LADIES' LETTER.

MY DEAR NELLIE, - I find from very close observations which I have made that many of the fashionable walking dresses are made without neck-bands, being cut round at the base of the throat and finished with a lace edging, and some kind of a ruffle or boa is gener- ally worn out of doors. Cravats of silk-muslin with edgings of lace, bows of white tulle, and scarves of lace tied in sailor knots or passed through gold or enamelled rings, are all fashionable, besides the Pierrot ruffs of black or white muslin and the chiffon boas with many long streamers of satin or velvet ribbon. Throatlets of black velvet with gold or jewelled clasps are. frequently worn with the low-cut collars, and are very becoming. A pretty bodice underneath goes a very long way to make a pleasant picture.
• I find that many popular hats are really the styles that were so prominent during the early zummer, with one important difference, viz., that the frilled brim is not made of thin chiffon, muslin,

.or silk, but of the more substantial linen, each frill -being corded or stitched at the edge. The high -crown is generally of coarse straw, but a few anodels have corded linen crowns also, and all are rnsually trimmed with folds of glace silk. Fancy ebra,ws in picturesque shapes are also greatly in Flavour, especially in shades of biscuit, tan, and cream, as well as in pale greens. They are very simply trimmed, as a rule, with folded bands and Zig bows of glace, or broad tinselled ribbon, but the bows need to be very smartly made and mounted to be in accordance with fashion. A hat of very pale green straw, trimmed with black glace, a couple of jet buckles, and a knot of pink c arnations under the bent-up brim is very pretty, and could be inexpensively copied by a clever milliner, as might another stylish hat of the [French sailor shape in burnt straw, which is trimmed round the crown with just a wreath of shaded pink-and-cream roses, alternating with -cream tulle rosettes. White chip hats, trimmed with white glace and white wings, are charming lar young girls' wear.

A very pretty blouse can be made with a slip of cream China silk, with a transparent yoke and long sleeves of cream lace, or of the thin silk, with transparent lace insertions let into it. It would Rot be quite in keeping to have a low neck and short sleeves, for a young girl. Another alterna- tive would be an entire 'blouse slip of creamy Re- naissance or other thin lace, with a low-necked and short-sleeved underslip of palest green or cream China silk to match the highest shade of the foliage. A cream lustre dress might have a plain skirt, trailing slightly at the back, and a bodice of Lire same, trimmed at the neck and end of the elbow sleeves with accordion-pleated frills of cream chiffon, and the blue lustre might be made with a little tucked or piped coat with a broad collar, vest, and sleeves of creamy lace.

really do not think that there is anything prettier than quite white hair, and there are very few faces to which it is not becoming—even young faces; but you will not be able to whiten your hair without using a strong bleach. Very strong chemi- cals have to be used for this purpose generally, so that sooner or later the hair loses its vitality al- together, and is quite destroyer], and the general health is affected also, so I certainly will not take the responsibility of advising the use of anything of this kind. And I think you will be most foolish to attempt anything yourself, leave Nature to do its own work; your hair will lose its colour quite soon enough, and it is far better to let it do so in its own time rather than do anything which might injure your health or your hair. As to the most fashionable coiffure of the moment, it is undoubtedly arranged with a side parting in front, while the waved hair is drawn up into a little twist on top ; for though efforts were made at the beginning of the season to alter the position of this coil or twist, and bring it low down in the neck, it made the average woman look so hopelessly dowdy that it never really became an accepted fashion. You can, with an easy mind, go dressing hair in your usual way, though if the kw coil suits your hats better, it will be equally correct if you adopt this style on other occasions. always think, however, that in the matter of &easing one's hair one should be guided more by what is becoming to one's particular type of face than 'by what is strictly fashionable. It is always easy to modify or adapt the style slightly. Your loving J ENNIE.

mother's sfae, and wondered. It was painted Wood, that was all. Just a bit of lifeless stick carved into the likeness of child. Ttg eves were trills,. and stared vacantly at her, the* was no volition, no intelligence, no soul in the poor little thing. But then it was declared miraculous by the Pops himself; it was crowned by the Vatican Council, its power was claimed by Cardinals and Bishops, it was venerated in one of the most renowned churches in Rome.
She left the room hurriedly, and came back to the room where Brother Francis and Rutland were

"Yes," the old priest was saying, "the sainted Bambino has had a most remarkable history. was carved by one of four brothers in Jerusalem. The wood was cut from the Mount of Olives. Doubtless this tree must have been at some time associated with our Blessed Lord. After he had carved it he was ordered to Rome, and so he had a box made, and brought it with him. While on the a dreadful storm arose, and there was great —e.nger lest the vessel and all hands on board should be lost. The captain gave orders that every- thing in the shape of baggage should be thrown overboard. This was done, and everything imme- diately sunk beneath the waves except the box con- taining the figure which our brother had carved. After a time the captain and the crew noticed that wherever the ship went the box followed. Someone said that it belonged to a Franciscan friar. Our brother was called, who immediately told the captaia that if the box was taken aboard the ship should be saved, and all hands should safely arrive at Naples. "The blessed Bambino was taken on to the boat and immediately the storm ceased. As you may imagine, the joy among the sailors was very great, and they all of them knelt before the figure which had saved them from death.

"When our brother reached Rome, he found that news of the wonderful child had gone before him, and the Aracceli was simply thronged with people to see it. Sick people came and went away well, and then our brothers at the monastery saw that the blessed Bambino had healing power. After that he was taken to the houses 'of sick people, and immediately they got well. No matter to whom he was taken, rich or poor, noble or humble, wherever he was received with faith he Bealed the people." Brother Francis took a pinch of snuff, and t^oked towards his listeners to see what impression nil tale was making. He noticed that Alizon was watching him with wondering eyes, and that Rutland sat looking on the ground. ".Ah, but," went on Brother Francis, "there were those who took advantage of the kindness of our Church, and the healing powers of the sainted Bambino. One day a woman came to us telling us that her child was ill, and asked that the Bambino be brought. Nothing doubting, our brothers took it to the woman's house and left it there. The ivoman's child got better, and so three days afterwards our brothers went for the image of the infant Jesus. The woman said she had carefully packed it in the box, and it was taken back to the church and put behind the altar. When all the brothers had got to bed that night they were awakened by someone knocking at the monastery door. One got up and looked out. It was a hitter cold night, and freezing hard. "` Who's knocking asked Brother Philip, who had got up. "But the only answer he heard was the cry of a child. Brother Philip immediately went down- stairs and opened the door, and there he saw the blessed Bambino, who had come all the way through the cold night. "Dien we all saw how the woman had deceived us. She had made an image in the likeness of the one we had tal en to her and had kept the real one. But the blessed Child, seeing how the brothers had been deceived, came back of its own accord." 3rother Francis ceased, and took another pinch of snuff.
"I suppese there is ro doubt about this story?" asked Alizon.

"Doubt, my child ? Oh, no Ever since that timEt two bro!hers havc. always accompanied the blessed It is always brought in a carriage, and taken nin th,? same way." "And how long need it. stay in my mother's room ? " asked Alizon.

"if she continues better in the morning I should say it would be long enough," replied Brother Francis. "With your consent, I will lie on the sofa until the morning." Sister Mary Calllo in the room. "Her ladyship it much better," she said. "She is sleeping like an infant, and the-, blessed Bambino is by her side. Oh, it is beautiful! beautiful!" _ _ _ _

"Then surely you can rest," said Rutland, turning to Alizon, "you may sleep in peace now!" Alizon answered him by a wan smile, and then found her way to her mother's room. Lady Neville was sleeping quietly. The fever had much abated, and her whole appearance bespoke a change for the better.
"Thank God! thank Godt" she ejaculated. "Yes, I can rest now."

She went to the drawing-room where Brother rorancis lay on the sofa. His mouth was wide open, and he snored vigorously. Alizon could not help smiling, for a more grotesque form it would difficult to conceive, it would 'be difficult to find a man whose personal appearance suggested spiritual things less than that of Brother Francis. His red pimply skin, his widely-extended mouth, and his fat, stodgy figure, told of good living and freedom from care. It was impossible to conceive that this man had ever grappled with intellectual difficulties, or faced the great problems of the spiritual world. The girl was about to leave the room when she caught sight of a book lying .on the table. On examining it she at first gave a start, then cast a hasty glance around the room. *Yes, she was unobserved; no one was there but the sleeping priest. With hurried steps she went to her bed- room, taking the book with her. Arrived there she examined the room as though she were afraid, but after making sure that she was alone she locked the door, and then drawing a wicker-chair under the electric light, she sat down and buried her face in her hands. For more than an hout she sat thus, Evidently she was thinking deeply, and when presently she lifted her head, her eyes shone with a strange light. She rose from her chair, and for some time walked to and fro in the room, then she sat down and began reading the book she had brought with her. "Mr. Rutland must have left it there," she said. "Yes, it is his, his name is on the title-page." ;i•or a little time she seemed to be in doubt about something; she was evidently nervous, too, for her %land trembled like an aspen leaf. "I can't sleep," she cried, impatiently, "I must do something. I will go into mother's room again." The girl hurried out, locking the door behind her, and a few seconds later she was standing by her mother's bedside. _ _

- - Lady Neville was still sleeping quietly. There could be no doubt about it she was much better. By her side was the grotesque little figure of the wooden Bambino, whose glassy eyes seemed staring into vacancy. Alizon turned away hurriedly, and returned to her bedroom again, locking the door. Taking up Rutland's book again she read for more than two hours. Evidently she was much interested, for she turned the leaves hurriedly, never lifting her eyes from the pages. When she had finished she glanced around the room like one afraid. She looked at her watch, and her eyes expressed wonder. "I had no idea it was so late," she said, pulling up the blind. The Aun was rising in a clear sky, all nature was awaking into life. She fell beside her bed, and remained kneeling until she heard someone knocking at her door.
CHAPTER XXII.
SIGHT-SEEING.

'4res days later Lady Neville, although still pronounced by the doctors to be out of danger. Her illness had been short, but it had severe. Brother Francis attributed her speedy recovery to the healing power of the Bambino, Sister Mary uttered many pious ejaculations, and praised the virtues of the sainted child. The other nurse smiled scornfully, while the doctors shrugged their shoulders. _ _ _

"Pah," said the Italian physician, "did I not say that we should cure her and the doll would get the credit? But what does it matter?" and he laughed contemptuously. Meanwhile the Bambino was taken back to the Francescan Church and placed in its little cabinet behind the altar. Rutland said nothing about Lady Neville's cure, and Alizon was also very reticent. She was over:ioyed at her mother's return to health, but spoke to no one concerning the means which had been used. Indeed, she seemed anxious to abstain from all reference to the Bambino, for when one day Sister Mary, the pious Catholic nurse, assured her ladyship that her recovery had been a miracle, and then looked to Alizon for con- firmation of her words, the girl left the room hastily without replying. For several days Rutland scarcely saw her. She

remained in close attendance on her motner, and did not appear in the public rooms even at dinner. And so the young man continued his tours around Rome, sometimes in company with Father Matthew. sometimes alone. He said nothing con Oerning his opinions, of what he saw, but he was none the less observant. He asked Many questions and 'took careful note of the answers given. Evidently, too, he was deeply impressed. On one occasion when Father Matthew accompanied him to the great Church of St. John's Lateran, where a number of young priests were ordained, the Jesuit observed that he never took his eyes away from the officiating Bishop, and. the young men who claimed that morning to be endowed with priestly power. "Very impressive, isn't it ? " asked Father Matthew.

'it is exceedingly interesting," replied Rutland, ~git although Father Matthew asked him many -eions he did not tell him what he really. taiought of the gorgeous ceremonial. Also when visiting the renowned Jesuit _Church of Rome, and the rooms where Ignatius Loyola srote his famous Constitution, he seemed like one in a trance. Father Matthew had difficulty in Ating him away. He went from one room to another, and then revisited them as if anxious that nothing should escape him. Especially did he linger in the apartment where Ignatius saw a vision of the Trinity, and where a picture, which translated the vision to canvas, was exhibited. He asked many questions concerning the circumstances which attended the vision, and appeared much die-. appointed at the vague answers given. Then again, when examining the many relics for which this, the headquarters of the Jesuits, is famous, he asked for some proof of their miraculous power, he was evidently much disappointed in the priest's replies. "Oh, there can be no doubt about their healing power," Father Matthew would say again and again. "Yes, but what proof do you offer to a sceptic ? " "Well, now," replied the priest, "take this finger. It belonged to a most holy nun. There was a movement set on foot for her beatification, and, of course, before this could be done it had to be proved that the nun, whose name was Teresa, had worked a miracle. Well, this finger," and the priest pointed to a bit of dried bone which lay sender the glass case before them, "had been pre- served. it was taken to a woman who the doctors. iared was dying, and immediately it was placed. in the dying woman's hand she got well." "Who was the woman ? " "I really don't know." "Where did she live ? " "Here in Rome." "How long ago ? " "Oh, sixty or seventy years since."' "But you don't know her name?'" ."Oh, n 0.,, "But who were the doctors who declared that she was dying ? " , "I really don't know." "But did they sign a certificate to the effect that the. woman was dying?"
"I really never -thoiight of it." "Do you know if these doctors-were deeply learned in the laws of haalth, and in the science of medicine ? "

"Oh, there can be no doubt they would be. You see, Teresa was made a saint, and consequently the matter would be carefully investigated. The Devil's Advocate would see to it that every point was discussed. Why, it took a long time to prove the case; indeed, it is one of the most expensive cases of the century. It cost over three thousand pounds." "Cost over three thousand pounds to make a. saint! How ? "

" Well, you see, when the desire was expressed' to make her a saint, there was a lot of opposition, - 'he part of the Devil's Advocate. You see, ...Ire are always two advocates appointed by the• Church when there is an attempt made for the canonisation, of beatification of anyone. One, 4dvocate argues in favour of the holiness, and the miraculous power of the departed one; and the other argues against it. The latter is called the Devil's Advocate. Of course, a Council of the Church is. called to adjudicate • and thus you see what with fees paid to the advocates, to the Council, and to the Holy. Father, it becomes a very expensive matter. In this,case there was-much controversy, and it swallowed up over three thou• - sand pounds." "Of course, this money goes to the funds of the- Church ? "
"Of course; and to the advocates." "I see. That is always the ease, whether the man or woman is made a saint or not? "

"Certainly." The foregoing is a sample of many of.the con- versations which took place as Rutland visited one sacred shrine after another. The young minister gave no opinion on anything he saw or heard; but he was evidently deeply impressed. When Lady Neville was sufficiently recovered, she asked Rutland to dine with her in her private. dining-room, and the young man, although almost dreading spending the evening with Alizon, con- sented. Try as he might he could not destroy the love which he again and again told himself was madness. And thus it was while it gave him pain to be near her and to speak with her, he was unable to resist the spell which she had cast upon him. No man knows how weak he really is until he falls- !n love. Then, in many cases, reason goes by the board, and men who are sane and,strong in; other. matters, become the sport of passing impulses. "I am afraid," said Lady Neville, during the. evening, "that Alizon is having what the Lanca- shire people call a weary time.' " "No, mother," cried Alizon,, "I am very happy now you are getting well." "I don't like your pale cheeks, my darling," said her ladyship, "and yet I am not strong enough to take much exercise."

"Can I be of any service ?." asked Rutland, "If Miss Alizon will accompany me on my journeys around the city, I shall be delighted." "No, no, mother," cried. Alizon, "I do not wish to leave you. lam much happier with you." "But there is no reason why you. should stay with me, my dear," said her ladyship. "It is a. fortnight now since I was taken ill, and in. that time you have scarcely left my side." "I have a. splendid excursion mapped, out for to-morrow," said Rutland mentioning various renowned places he, intended visiting. "Can you resist such a programme ?" said Lady Neville, smiling. "I feel I must accept Mr. Rutland's kindness for you, if you will not do, so .r yourself."' The girl's eyes kindled as Duncan mentioned the places he intended to visit, and yielding to the impulse of the moment, she accepted. Rutland had now been more than a month in Rome, and was becoming acquainted with the 41ty. He had also been able to pick up a smatter- ing, of the language, and could read the Italian papers without much difficulty. Each day, more- over, he was understanding more and more, the spell which Rome casts upon all who really breathe her atmosphere. Ile felt the truth of the saying that no man could understand the history of civilisation until he- had spent some time in Rome. He was now sufficiently strong to bear a day's sight-seeing without being fatigued, and it was with a fast-beating heart that he took his seat beside Alizon on the following morning, and told the cabman to drive to St. John's Lateran. He felt that the gulf between himself and Alizon was deepening and widening. Rome was affecting him in many ways, and in spite of their being thrown together by Lady Neville's illness he knew that Alizon was less frank with him than she had been during the first part of her stay in Rome. Close to St. John's Lateran is a little church 'called the Santa Scala, or the Church of the Sacred Steps. It is so named because it is ascended by a number of steps which St. Helena brought from Jerusalem. These steps, it was asserted, were those on which our Saviour trod when leaving '• house. it Duncan and Alizon arrived here they Father Matthew awaiting them. -..tiis place is most interesting," said the priest. Mioever goes up these steps has one thousand ;-ears' indulgence granted."
_ " se A then are two sets of steps up to the .7..nrch," said Rutland.

"441 i yes, but it.is only these on the right by which jou gain the indulgence. Look at those people." The sight was indeed interesting; for just before them were about thirty people going up the marble stairway on their knees. F.,!otne were stoop- ing and kissing the cold stones. "You see," went on the priest, "the only way to get the indulgence is to go up on your knees. Indeed, you are not allowed to ascend any other
4A. thousand years," said Duncar.. "It is a long time."

"-Yes, one of the Popes granted this great favour." "Have you ever ascended them 1` " asked Rutland. "No, I never have." The young minister smiled, but he s cthin. Alizon looked at his face steadily, Of if she wished to read his thoughts.

Tnenu urown, ,-frlic's will fizure in the coronation ceremonies of the new King of Italy, is not exactly all that its name would imply. What little iron there is in it, is supposed to have been beaten out into 4 thin circle from one of the nails used at the Crucifixion, and the crown thus formed is richly Eet in gold and jewels. It is regarded as one of the most precious heirlooms of the Italian Royal House, though it seems to have had many varying fortunes. Originally it was bestowed by Pope Gregory the Great, upon Queen Theodolinda under whom the Lombards first changed their faith for the Catholic belief. Charlemagne,and Henry of Luxemburg were crowned with it, and it was also used in more modern times at the coronstion of Napoleon I. Subse- quently it passed into the possession of Austria, and the Emneror Francis Joseph, restored it to the ling of Italy, in 1866. _

Queen Helene, like the Dowager Queen Marguerite. is an ardent mountaineer,never seeing a mountain without longing to climb it. She is, too, an enthusiastic yachts- woman, and a magnificent shot. It is said that her father has frequently offered to let her shciot an apple off his head, but be this as it may Queen Be ele is never known to miss her mark.

It is about twenty-five or thirty years, since society women took to shooting. The Comtesse de Paris was Probably the first woman of title who went out regularly with gun and dog for a day's sport. Now, in these days, there are any number of six4rtswomen, many of whom are quits as expert with the gun as their husbands and brothers. There are some even, who, like Mrs. Alan Gardner, go in for big glme shooting, and who visit India, Africa, and other parts for this purpose. There are of course many good sportswomen who do not shoot. Severa! of the Princesses of our Royal Family, might b. included in this category, but none of them go in regu- larly for shooting. For ordinary sport, the Duchess of Bedford is usuallr regarded as the best all-round shot, while there are few of either sex who are more success- ful at deer stalking than Lady Tweedmouth or Lady Breadalbane.

The Paris" Revue des Revusa " has been encouraging for the heliday season, a discussion of the question whether or not the increasing attention paid by women to outdoor sports, will be prejudicial to their future. This is one of the questions which cannot be answered by a direct negative or affirmative, seeing that it depends very much upon the na,ure of the outdoor sports. and many other considerations. However the correspondents of the Parisian paper offer various opinions, and M. Emile Zola is good enough to say of of Englishwomen that " however uninteresting they may be on foot, I always watch them pedalling to market with the greatest pleasure." Such a criticism reining from a man who was the guest of Britain when France treated him unkindly, does not strike one as too generous, and the reference to cyclists " pedallinry to market" eeerns to show that the distinguishei French- man's observations have been rather superficial. But, regarding the general question, there appears to be a concensus of opinion that the practice of athletics is not prejudicial to women, and no doubt that is the correct view, so long as the exercise, is taken with reasonable moderation, and is of a kind suitable to women. The woman cyclist in" rationale" has never been a pleasing or taking spectacle in this country. To some extent sha has bean tolerated in the South, hut when a touring Englishwoman recently appeared in a famous and historical city in Scotland, riding a man's machine, she soon discovered that there is a strong popular pre- judice aarainst unwomanly clothes" in the North. Even in France, where nearly every French woman cyclist wears " rationale they sometimes meet with protest. At Rouen Cathedral, for instance, the chief priest recently, put up a notice that no wonaan would be admitted in " unseemly garments." As the famous Cathedral is a 'neat centre of attraction this was rather awkward for the large number of crelisrm who visit it. The verger however soon rose to the occasion, and settled the difficulty to everybody's satisfaction, by providing skirts on hire. For this accommodation he charges one franc elch, and it is said that be is rapidly amassing a fortune.

It is welcome intelligenee that a new nrefessership has been established at Newnham College, and that it has tven conferred upon the scholarly Miss .;ane Harrison. But it is not to the authorities of the University that Newnham owes its fellowship, the necessary fund having been collected by the associates of the College. Both Oxford and Cambridge maintain their unen- lightened attitude towards women students, to whom they refuse degrees, however great the distinction with which the examinations may be passed. It is strange indeed that this anomaly should he retained in England, where three Snverigns since Eiward VI. have been women, two of them amongst the very greatest rulers that the country has seen. Recent heat wave—not confined to this country— have induced an Amerlcan to bring nut a new sunshade with a revolving fan attached t the handle. The fan opens and shuts with the parasol, and it is rotated be means of a little mechanical arrangement, which can be easi!v nnerated by one of the fingers. It not only keeps off the sun. hut also produces a sensible brerze with very little effort. This new invention Seems to 1) a little late for our summer, thrrugh we may yet have plenty of hot weather. But it is tot, as a rule, nut of doors that we most feel the need of an artificial breeze, even in the hottest weather, and there is scarcely likely to be a great de- mand for the new sensherle, especially when we consider the risk of destructive effects to our headgear and reifies—by the revolving "arrangement. The idea no doubt, cernes from the East. In India and China, the electrically driven revolving fan,ia gradually ousting the old-fashioned punkah, and the punkah-wallah,—that much abused individual in familiar te all Anglo Indians. The tightly-fitting sleeve is doomed, a graceful looseness charaeterising all those built for Autumn wear. Undoubtedly this is a mere becoming style to the majority, but it is neverthrleas to he honed that we shall not again revert to the " baloon " variety, that it is not " the thin end of the wedge." The " c'oed " sleeve is in great favour for dinner and evening frocks. The fabric displayed is semi tr tneparent, such as chiffon, or cf 6ae de Chine, and it is stt into the armhole with fine gaugings. What with the fav,urite simple steno:v. with a big ribbon how, and the capelineove have ail apneared very youthful this summer anent the heal. That, frequeetly, the faces beneath the babyish headgear were far in advance of youthful (!ays,seemed trouble the wearers not one whit. Now, however. we shill have to begin to turn nut attention to more solid strectures, and very delightful they premise to prove. Tartan panne, and ribbon, are in great reve:t by leading milliners j Ist now. It is almost always thns at this se is-in of the year, when we have grown weary of so much softn-ss and uniformity of colouring. Numerous cases of font poisoning reported at the hospitals affirm the importance of wearing only fast dyed hose. This is infinitely more important in summer than in winter, as the freer wrspiratinn causes the abzorptien of the poisonous dyes se frequently need in the commoner qualities of hosing. Tnis le especially the case in the highly-cotoered deserintiens, and in the majority of the case reported at tb,e hosnitel the colour of the socks or e'ockings has been rel. Tills class of hosiery is wre injarious, and in the case of a cut, or slight scratch, it max easily lead to the most serious form of bloelnalicoling. The safer plan, if the wearer is unable t afford the hest fast dyed qualities, is to buy hose that is not dyed at all. " MADGE•"

div.head: SWIMMING.
div.p: SWIMMING.
The Quarter-Mile Championship of St. Helens.
Burrows Beaten by Kearsley

There was a good at' Wance at the St.Helens Corpora- tion Baths on Tuesday night, to witnrss the race for the Quaater-mile Championship of the St. Helens Swim- ming Club. Keen excitement was manifested in the event on account of the fact that W. Burrows (last Year's winner) had a stronger swimmer to meet in Fred Kearsley, who finished sth in the 1.000 yards champion- ship race at Blackpool on Saturday. T. Green and R. Heaton also took part in the quarter-mile race, which was for the Licensed Victuallers' Challenge Trophy. A good start was made at five minutes past eight, Bur- rows leading off. with Kearsley close behind , Green being third. For three lengths this order wa maintained, Burrows being about five yards ahead 0 f Kearsloy, who was swimming in capital style. After this Kearslev gradually overhauled his man, and at the end of the fourth length passed the holder, amid excite- ment, eventually winning by a length. Burrows was second, and Green third. Heaton retired about half- way throut h. Kearslev finished the distance (thirteen lengths Of the bath) in 6min. 22sees• Burrow's timo was ! 6min. 53secs. The Rev Canon Willink afterwards pl.( - tented the shield, and said that K,arslev had won it in a handsame fashion, and the way in which he swam the thirteen lengths had gained him an enviable distinction. A two lengths' squadron race (six a-side) was decided between St. Helens and Leigh, the former winning by about ei ht yards. To cenclu le the prozramme a water polo match was played between St. Helens 2nd and Leigh Ist, with the following result r—St. Fielens 2nd 12 goals, Leigh Ist nil.

div.head: TRAINING AND OVER-TRAINING.
div.p: TRAINING AND OVER-TRAINING.
Amateur Rider's Views.

In these days of "Long Ride" Championships, when miles by the thousand are put to the credit of many a rider, facts anent a hundred-mile ride over singularly bad roads by Mr. Samuel Len:lard. will not he without interest to cyclists all over the country. Mr. Lennard,wha resides at 2,Canaliann-road, Fulham, is by trade a d-‘corator, but being of an inventive turn and possesein some skill as an engineer, he a few years since made a bicycle with celain improvements of his own. The success attending his efforts brought him in contact with nun.erous riders, and he was induced to join a club. "I have always worked hard all Riv life," sail Mr. Lennard, "and .the hard work of training did not dis- tress me. There la a great deal of harm in over• training, but although I have lately been ill. my illness was in no way caused by over-training. I had entered for a club race from London to .Reading. I trained slowly and carefully ; hut it was by no means an ideal day for cycling when the day of the race was reached. It was heavy and wet travelling, and at Slough I had to give in. I can hardly ex• plain what was wrong, hut I felt queer and out cf sorts, with pains in my back, and when I got home I was forced to go to bed. A doctor was sent for and it was found that I had contracted a had attack of pnen- nannia, with pleurisy. For something like six week a I hovered between life and death ; but afterwards I gradually cammended to mend, until I was able to get up and about. The worst part of my illness was the shortness of my breath when I breathed I felt just as if a needle was running through my lungs. My doctor said I should get better in time, but I found it was a very long time. I looked more fit for my coffin than to be nut in the street. I went to the hospital and they gave me medicine, hut I found no relief, until one day I met Mrs. Duncan, a reat've of mine, who advised me to buy a hox of Dr. Williams' pink pills fe) pale people, which had cured many cases like my own, and Said that if I carried out the instructions carefully I should soon find an improvement. That very nicht I commenced taking them. Before that box was empty I felt already better. My breathing improved, and I could walk and eat better; and so I went on gradually until I began to think of starting work again. My friends never then7ht they would see me working this; side of the grave, but I went on with Dr. Williams' pink pills until 1 felt so well that I started riding again. Within nine weeks of commencing the pills I entered for a race,and won after a very hard tussele : there is the prize—a marble cleck. If it had not been for Dr. Williams' pink pills I shon'd never have won that. I went on improving, so that I really thought I would come out as a professional rider ; and in order to see what I really nnuld d,, I trained my. self carefully. taking Dr. Williams' pink pills all the while,and after four weeks I went in for a long-distance ride, and I scenmnlilhed fifty-two miles in three hours and a little under the quarter. Six of us started, and I did the fifty-two miles in the quickest time any mem- ber of our club has ever done it. They chaffed me about the pills. but I went on taking them, and when they nresented me with that medal there, they asked me if I was going to give it to Dr. Williams." 4. Wind," the athlete's first need, simply means lung- power : and it is remarkable Oat Mr. Lennerd, after suffering specifically from shortness of breath, shou'd have attained eminence in a sport making such demands upon the tuners, as bicycling. But shortness of breath is a frequent eynnot om of anaemia (or deficient blood- supnlv), and Dr. Williams' pink pills have a well-earned celebrity for increasing and enrichiny, the blood, and curing all disorders which arise from its deficiency. Other diseases they have cured incTude paralysis, rheumatism, sciatica, rickets, indigestien, nalpitations. all forms of female weakness and hysteria They are cenuire only with full name, Dr. Williams' pink pills for rale neonate, anrl are sold by Dr. Williams' Medicine Company, flnlhorn Viadnet, London, at two shillings and ninepenee a box, or six boxea for thirteen and fire, poet free ; also by chemists. They are a wholesome and powerful tonic, invigorating after over- work or worry.

New Departure at St. Helens —Bricks made
of Glass and Sand

For years scient;sts and chemists have endeav- oured to discover the means of turning to account immense heaps of spent sand and glass resulting from the operation of griiviing plateglass. This waste material is conaPosed of ninety-seven per cent of ground glass rind spent sand—sea sand— which has been used for grinding, the remainder being iron worn from runners At the immense works of Pilkington Bros., 1,5(10.000 tons of this matter has accumulated, and 1200, tons are added we4cly to the ponderous triound,wlv4re Dr.Ormondy has discover-od, after much research and experi- ment, practicable means of making serviceable bricks. It appears that the presence of iron doss not interfere with the making of bricks, which will be wed not only for building porpose4, but fcr special operations which have hitherto necessitated peculiar material. The bricks have withstood ex- ceptionally severe tests, and a few months will see their introduction to th world, Messrs. Pilkington Brothers having laid down plant at their works, where the process of manufacturing the new bricks will SCI3II be in full swing.

div.head: TEMPTATION OF DUNCAN RUTLAND.
div.p: THE TEMPTATION OF DUNCAN RUTLAND.
By JOSEPH HOCKING,
Author of "The Birthright," "Mistress Nancy Molesworth," "All Men are Liars," "The Story of Andrew Fairfax," &c.
CHAPTER XXI.
HOW THE BAMBINO CURED LADY NEVH,LE.

Rutland led the way while the brown-frocked friars carried their precious burden along the corridors of the hotel and up to her ladyship's room. Most of the visitors had gone to bed, and none but the few waiters I h o watched the proceed- ings, some with awe, and others with a look of amusement, knew of the advent of the sacred relic. Brother Francis and Brother Anthony carried the thing into her ladyship's drawing-room, and then took off its many wrappings. Then when its outer adornments had bPen pulled aside, the little thing appeared to Rutland's gaze, just as it may be seen at the Church of The Aracceli (Altar of Heaven), by any visitor to Rome. He saw that it was about two feet long, and was lavishly decorated with gaudy ornaments. The young man looked at. the relic long and steadily, while the monks knelt before it and muttered a prayer. The figure of the little child interested him greatly, not simply I),....cause of the stories told about it, but because of he system of which it formed a part. This little inanimate figure was blessed by the Pope, a pamphlet had been written on its virtues, and issued with the approval of the ecclesiastical authorities. He had gone into the Via Condotti after dinner, and had bought a picture of the image, and had carefully read the inscription and the prayer which was associated with it. On trans- lating the former, which was written in French, he read as follows:

"Prayer in honour of the infant Jesus, whose miraculous image is venerated within the Church of the Altar of Heaven in Rome, and crowned by the Authorities of the Vatican on May 2nd, 1897. The Pope and the Authorities of the Vatican then had declared the little wooden figure to be miraculous; therefore it formed a part of the faith of the Church. As the priests knelt before it, he could not help thinking of the second Command- ment, and of the battle-cries of the sturdy Protes- tants of the Netherlands. He saw, moreover, that the Bambino had a round, badly-carved face, and was altogether destitute of beauty ; but no part of the body could be seen because it was covered with gaudy apparel. On its head was a crown sur- mounted by a cross that glittered with jewels. On every part of the body gaudy coloured stones had been placed. gold chain was hung around its., neck, and on its little arms all sorts of baubles:: were placed. The clothes which covered the] shapeless form were decorated with all sorts of; designs wrought in gold and precious stones. On its breast was a glittering star, while at the part' of the form where the knees should be, a cross was placed, and underneath the letters 1.11. S. were. traced in shining stones. While he looked Alizon entered. "Is this it? " she asked.

"Yes, my child," said Brother Francis, "I was able to prevail on our Superior to let me bring the Holy Child to your mother's bedside." Alizon looked at it like one fascinated. She had been bred a Catholic, and had been taught to believe in Catholic legends ; but as she gazed at the. little thing a cold feeling came into her heart. A chilling wave of doubt swept over her. What good could this poor little doll do to her mother? It, was only painted wood covered with tinselled drapery and gaudy ornaments. What miraculous power could it have? Was it not foolishness, yes, ; worse than foolishness, was it not blasphemy to fall down before the senseless object and offer prayers? But this was only for a second. She drove her doubts from her. Who was she to doubt what th, Holy Father and the Vatican Council had declared miraculous? "Will you take it in at. once!" she said. The two monks carried the Bambino into the sick- room and placed it on the bed. Lady Neville looked towards them as they entered, but there was no look of intelligence in her eyes.l The priests performed the customary rites, but she heeded them not. She was moaning something about the deer parks around the Priory, and then she spoke of Sir Charles Neville, her late husband.; "Tier hand has touched the hand of the blessed Bambino," said Brother Francis presently. "By the blessing of our Holy Mother, she will get better." Meanwhile Sister Mary was frantically praying,,z the other nurse looking on with a scornful smile. For a few minutes Alizon watched. She had heard how in olden times when the sick had touched even the robe of Christ that virtue went out of. Him and He healed them. But her mother had! touched this figure, and nothing had happened. "Oh, she will diet" thought the girl, "my-. mother will die!" Ordinarily Alizon was self-possessed; but the _ _ _

thought of -losing her mother -had unnerved her,l while the continuous moanings of Sister Mary had' made the young girl anticipate the most terriblei things. An hour passed away, during which time the monks remained, and the Bambino lay on the bed beside her ladyship; but the patient seemed worse rather than better. The fever rose rather than abated, and she talked more inces,antly, more incoherently. "Be patient, my child," said Brother Francis, as he noted Alizon's grief; "the Blessed Child will heal her."
"It is time her ladyship took her medicine," said the nurse who had not participated in the rites. _

"There is no need," said Sister Mary. "I obey the doctors, " replied the woman, pouring out the medicine. She gave it to her ladyship, and then retired from the bedside. About half-an-hour later the patient became better, and fell asleep. "Did I not tell you?" said Brother Francis. "Her recovery is beginning. I take this as an omen from Heaven. _
Sister Mary sobbed out her thankfulness, and the two priests spoke to each other in Italian; but Alizon spoke no word. In her eyes was a strange expression. Bewilderment, faith, doubt were all there.

Meanwhile Duncan sat in the drawing-room. He had slept a little through the day; 'but only a little. The thought of Alizon's anguish made rest almost possible. He was anxiously awaiting news, for he was afraid lest all the excitement should hinder her ladyship's recovery rather than help it. Presently Alizon and Brother Francis returned. "Mother is better," said the girl. "For an hour or so she seemed worse, but she has fallen asleep now." "Yes," said the sceptical nurse, who had followed them, having to fetch something from the drawing-room, "the medicine I gave her is very soothing," Brother Francis looked at her indignantly, but said nothing. He disliked this woman very much. "Yes," he said, "her ladyship is better. Ah, it is not the first tin:e I have taken the blessed Bambino to work its cures."

Rutland did not reply, he felt the utter useless- ness of saying what he thought to the old monk. Besides, why should he speak of his unbelief to Alizon If she derived comfort from the presence of tho wooden figure, he would not seek to take it away. And yet the whole episode was revelation of the mental condition of the Roman Church. From the Pope down to the brown-frocked friar, they all regarded the Bambino as a miraculous image. They venerated it, and believed in its healing power. "I am glad her ladyship is better," he said to Alizon. "I hope you will be persuaded to take a little rest now." -
"I cannot, I cannot." said the girl. "I shall not be able to sleep until I know that mother is out of danger. Yon see, everything has come on so suddenly, and—nnd lam all alone." .
"No, no, my child," said Brother Francis, "the blessed 'Virgin will be near to help you. Do not be afraid." •

Ilia girl started up and went to her mother's room. Lady Neville was still sleeping quietly, while beside her was the Bambino. Alizon thought of he own childhood's days when it comforted her to have a doll by her side when she went to bed. "You would have liked to have seen it, wouldn't you?" and he turned to Alizon. "Oh, yes! "said the girl. "Of course:you have proof that it is the true Cross?" CC Undoubted proof," said the priest. gg After St. Helena was converted, she found three Crosses one day, and she came to the conclusion that thei were the Crosses of Christ and the two thieves. Naturally she wished to discover which wits the Cross on which our Lord- hung. Near by was * sick man, and she took these Crosses-to him. She concluded that this was the- true Cross, and a part of it is in that church." The girl was silent. "On certain days," went on Father Matthew, "these relics are exhibited and people are grantect special indulgencies. lam sorry you cannot see them to-day. div.head: FREE CHURCHES.
div.p: THE FREE CHURCHES.
THE END OF THE " MAY " MEETINGS.

The " May " meetings go on from April to September. Among Nonconformists, the Wesleyan Methodist Conference" is commonly regarded as the last of them. The Conference this year at Burslem was not in any way re- markable except for the profound, impressive discussion on the Twentieth Century Fund. On this occasion Mr. Price Hughes excelled himself, and the other orators deeply touched the fathers and brethren. In the course of a very short time promises of an additional C 40,000 were made to the fund. We trust and believe that before the end of the year the million guineas will be raised. Dr. Allen, as was expected, was elected President, and acquitted himself admirably in the chair. Dr. Allen takes a keen interest in the Free Church Federation movement, and is an active member of the Birmingham Free Church Council. Next year be will be succeeded by Professor Davison, a former editor of the Methodist Recorder.

div.head: GREAT MISSION FOR ALL ENGLAND.
div.p: A GREAT MISSION FOR ALL ENGLAND.

That is how the Puritan describes the simul- taneous mission which is being organised by the National Free Church Council. Our con- temporary had an interesting article on the mission, illustrated by photographs of the Rev. Thos. Law, the Organising Secretary of the National Council; Rev. Dr. Maciaren, of Manchester; Rev. J. H. Jowett, MA., and others. "1901," says the writer, *" will be chiefly noticeable in the religious history of 'England for the most remarkable Evan- gelical crusade ever set on foot in this or any other country." Thousands of ministers and local preachers, inclu ding the most distin- guished men in the Free Churches, will lead the way, and two million Church members are being asked to keep the dates free from all other engagements. So far, the proposal has been taken up with enthusiasm; and though he has communicated with all the leading ministers •and missioners in the country, Mr. Law has received only one discouraging response. Mr. Law attaches the greatest importance to the village mission, which extends from March 2 Ito 6, inclusive. " Jealousies and prejudices," he says, "often exist in villages which are not ;known in the towns, and to bring all the Churches together in a mission will be the greatest possible blessing to them all."
SOUND DOCTRINE FROM A ROMANIST.

This headline will seem rather startling to our readers, but e can justify it. St. Alban's, Holborn, is one of the best known Highest of High Churches in England, and Father Stanton, one of the best known Highest of High Church clergymen. Yet, preaching in St. Alban's, Holborn, Father Stanton maintained that the true Church is to be found where two or three are gathered together in the name of Christ. We Free Churchmen have been proclaiming this for generations. But if it is true doctrine, as it is, what becomes of theories of apostolical succession, validity of orders, and the rest, by which High Anglicans and Roman Catholics have sought to exclude Nonconformists from the true Church of God? We hope Father Stanton will give himself heartily to the further study and exposition of Free Church principles.

div.head: MRS. W. P. HARTLEY.
div.p: MRS. W. P. HARTLEY.

'The September Free ,Churchman, of which we have seen ran advanced copy, contains a very interesting sketch by the Rev. J. Day Thomp- son, of Mrs. Hartley, wife of Mr. W. P. Hartley, IP., of Aintree, the great preserve manufac- turer and Primitive Methodist. The article is illustrated by a photograph of the subject, and of Mr. Hartley's house at Aintree. The writer says that Mrs. Hartley has helped her husband in his great work most by managing his home withwonde rful tact and skill, and by the careful training of their children. "I have it OD the authority of one of her daughters that for over a space of twenty years, while her children were young, she never left them for a single night, and it is beautiful to hear the reverent manner in which they now speak of her, and to observe the gentle but complete deference they pay to her."

THE RETIREMENT OF MII. CARVELL WILLIAMS. Mr. Carvell Williams, M.P., who is himself practically the Liberation Society, has inti- mated that he does not intend to contest the Mansfield Division at the next election. This • announcement will be received by Free Church- men with great regret. Mr. Carvell Williams is such a vigorous, lighthearted man, that it is difficult to realise that he is in his eightieth year. His seidress last spring, as chairman of the Congregational Union, was a pcwerful pro- nouncement. He has been connected with the Liberation Society for over fifty years. He first antered 'Pacliament as member for South Nottingham in 1885; but when Mr. Gladstone tppealed to the country :OD Home Rule some months . after the General Election, Mr. Williams was among those meno lost their seats. He was elected for the Mansfield Division in 1892. His work has been rendered particularly difficult of late by increasing deafness. •THE BISHOP AND THE 'WESLEYAN'S. The late Bishop 'Ryle of Liverpool, was on terms very good with the Free Churchmen of the city, and was a close friend of Charles Garrett. The Liverpool Wesleyan Methodist Council has sent:an address of welcome to Dr. Ryle's .successor, Bishop Chavasse, also an Evangelical. Dr. Chavasse has sent a gracious reply to the address. "I know," he says, "the happy relations whic,-h existed between my pro, decessor, Bishop Ryle, and the Wesleyan Church, and trust the same sense of brother— hood in Christ will be not less strongly felt in the future. The Church of Christ must close its ranks, and be at peace within itself, if it is to make any impression on the appalling mass of sin and isulifierenoe .by which it is sur- rounded."

div.head: REV. R. J. CAMPBELL, B.A.
div.p: REV. R. J. CAMPBELL, B.A.

Mr. Campbell is staying at Freshwater, Isle of Wight, and continues to gain strength, although his convalescence is somewhat slow and painful. He is now able to walk with the aid of a stick a few yards at a time. Mr. Campbell's return to active ministry at Brighton before October is quite improbable. His people will receive him again with joy and heartfelt gratitude.

div.head: IN AID OF THE INFIRMARY. To-Morrow's Parade znd Carnival.
div.p: IN AID OF THE INFIRMARY. To-Morrow's Parade znd Carnival.

A further meeting of the committee appointed to make arrangements for the Cycle Parade and Carni- val in aid of the Infirmary, which will be held on Saturday, took place last Thursday evening. Mr D Fanshaw presided over a representative attend- ance. It was reported that, in consequence of the short notice the Friendly Societies were unable to take part in the demonstration. The meeting de- cided to endeavour to obtain the services of the Lynam Morris Dancers, and the collecting system was thoroughly discussed. Ix addition to nand boxes long bamboo poles with bags attached, will be used. On Monday evening a meeting of ladies willing to take part in the collecting was held in the Town Hall, the Mayoress presiding, over an attendance ot about thirty. A gentlemen's deputa- tion attended the meeting, and a large number of ladies took collecting books. As we stated last, week efforts are being made to realise at least £2OO, and the demonstration will undoubtedly exceed anything of the kind previ- ously attempted in the town. The procession will leave the Town Hall at 5.30 p m and proceed along Sankey-street, Buttermarket-street, Irlam-street, Church-street to the lamp opposite the Parish Church,and then along Mersey street, Bridge-street, Horsemarket-street, IVinwick-street, Tanners-lane, Froghall-lane, Priestly-street, Powys-street, Liver- pool-road, Bank Quay Bridge. Parker-street, Wilson Patten-street, Bold-street, Palmyra Square to the Town Hall. The following organizations nave promised to take part in the parade :-Ist Volunteer Battalion South Lancashire Regi- ment Cycle Corps, Warrington Cycling Club, Warrington Royal Cycling Club, Warrington Thursday Cycling Club, Padgate Cycling Club Widnes Cycling Club, Widnes Wheelers Cycling Club, Warrington Cricket Club, Warrington ttu4by Football Club, Warrington Association Football, Club, Warrington Harriers, Sankey Harriers, mem- bers of the Gymnasium,St John Ambulance Brigade Warrington Fire Brigade,and most of the local brass bands. All cyclists in fancy dress are invited to take part. Prizes are offered for the most humorous and original "get-ups," best decorated machine, &c A selection of costumes by S. B. Watts and Co., of. Manchester, will be on view at the Patten Arms Hotel nest Thursday and Friday from 3 to 9 p m , and on Saturday, from 10 a.m to 3-30p.m. After the parade a grand smoking concert will be held in the Parr Hall when the prizes will be dis- tributed.

div.head: rHERE IS NOTHING SO GOOD AS RIZINE•
div.p: rHERE IS NOTHING SO GOOD AS RIZINE•

Rizine is prepared by a special scientific process. Rizine is a more easily digested food than rice, and at the Name time contains a larger percentage of avail able nutriment. Itzine contains more flesh-forming substances than rice, tapioca, arrowroot, and cornflJur. Rice is the favourite food of half the human race. It'zine is a better food.

Rizine is the most convenient form of food, and it should enter into the component parts of all dishes, as it is plain and inexpensive, and it can Le employed in a large number ot ways. Toe "British Medical Journal " says :—"Rizine is a light and easily digestible food." Sold everywhere in 3i and 6.1 packets only. A single trial will confirm our std.tement that "there is nothing so good as Rizine."

div.head: FOOTBALL CLUB SPORTS.
div.p: THE FOOTBALL CLUB SPORTS.
Glorious Weather and a Large Crowd.

That the Warringt—on Rugby Football Club Sports are as popular an event as ever with the public, was evident on Saturday afternoon, from the large concourse of spectators which assembled on the Wilderspool enclosure. Tie sports should have taken place on Bank Holiday, but, owing to the wretched weather that prevailed, were postponed. Much to the gratification of the committee Satur- day was a gloriously fine day and the ground was in capital condition. From shortly before two o'clock the turnstiles clicked merrily, and consider- ing that the festival was a postponed event, it re- ceived a satisfactory share of public patronage. There was a very large number of entries and keen com- petition was witnessed in the different events. The cycle races furnished the most excitement, and there were comparatively few "spills." The officials who discharged their onerous duties with ability were : Timekeeper, Mr J E Warren ; starter, Mr T Wain- wright ; judges, Messrs J W Dillon, J E Warren ; judge of boxing competition, Sergeant- Major Haigh ; committee, Messrs W Nevins, W Hewitt, J T Thornilev, F Heesom. T Barnes, J T Bate, W Hill, T Davies, J Hackett, and James T Bate ; handi- capper, Mr W Platt ; hon. treasurer, Mr T Pemberton ; hon. secretary, Mr Fl Ashton. The Boreugh Band was in attendance and enlivened the proceedings by render- ing selections in a creditable manner. At the close of the sports the prizes were presented to the successful competitors by the Mayor (Alderman Roberts) who apologised for the absence of the Mayoiess who was announced to distribute the awards. He also congratu- lated the promoters upon having had such a glorious day for the carrying out of the programme.
100 YARDS HANDiDAP.

There were ten heats in the opening sprint, the first in each heat running in the second round, and the first and second in each heat of the second round being eligi- ble to run in the final. After half a dozen heats had been run it was discovered that the competitors bad been coy-ring the " 100 yards "in less than nine seconds—a record time—the cause of this being that the distance had been under-measured. The heats had couqfquently to he run over aeain. Some good racing was witnessal, C Aihton, of 'Manchester, and J Hughes, el Flint. runningla dead heat J Cad- man, of Ard wick, a short, thick-set athlete, ran well and secured first place in the sth beat, but upon the heat being raced a second time he was beaten by W Weliings, of Prescot. J Barnes, of St. Helens, exhibited such fine form in the ninth heat, that it was thought to be practically a certainty that he would ob- tain the first place in the fieal. The conclusion was justified, for the S. Helens footballer led from the start in the final, and won by fully two yards from Prince, the local runner. The time recorded was 10 seconds. J. L. Hughes. of Flint, secured the third place. The competitors in the final of this event, rode at such a "crawling " pace, teat. after the first lap, the judges stopped the race, and the riders were told that unless they increased their rate of speed, no prize would be awarded. The spectators heartily approved of the action of the judges. T Astill, of Warringten, obtained third place in the final. The winner of the heats were :—First, 1, J P White, Manchester, 2. B Craze, Altrincham ; second. 1. J Haves, Salford, 2, C E Monk, Risley ; third. 1, W J Balsbaw, St. Helens, 2, T Astill, Warrington ; fourth,l, A Baguley, Csdishead, 2, H Bennett, Salford. In the final, J P White, Manchester (135) sailed home winner by four lengths, B Craze (155) coming in second and being followed, only a wheel behind. by T Astill (170). The time recorded was 2mins. 324ecs. The prizes awarded were :—First.liqu-r and game cabinet; second, case of silver-mmunted carvers ; third, silver-plated sardine frame.
.880 YARDS HANDICAP

The field was in fine condition for the half-mile nee,. E Hilton,of INl,.wton, fr ona the limit, Pcored by five yards from the two virtual scratch men,A B rtwistle,No:thwich (43),and T Burgess,Widnes (53),in 2fnin 2:l:ec. The prizes were : First, case of fruit combination (preserted by Messrs. Eustance and C)); second, silver-plated cake stand; third, silver plat( d tea pot. Two MILES BICYCLE HANDICAP. . _

This was undoubtedly the most interesting event of the afternoon. It was raced in three heats, the first and second in each heat ci moetine in the foal. There was some capital racing in the second heat, T Astill, the favourite local rider, coming out first after a stiff fight, amid tremendous applause. The ridin4of W Clarile, of Wigan, who was virtually scratch man, was the feature of the heat, this competitor securing the second place after some splendid work. The winners of heats were : First, 1, El Wilson, Manchester, 2, E Turvey, Liverpool ; second, 1, T Agin, Warrington, 2. W Clarke, Wigan ; third, 1, J P White, Manchester, 2. B Crag, Altrincham. In the final J P White (205). came in first, a length separating him from T Astill (260). W Clarke (155) obtained the third place. The time was 6rnin. 12secs. The prizes consisted of : First, gentlemen's complete fitted dressing bag ; sec )nd case of afternoon spoons, salt cellars, &c. ; third, silver- plated hot-water jug. ONE MILE FEAT HANDICAP. This event was a most exciting affair. Eighteen runners competed, and in the last lap the issue lay between J W Esstwood. Warrington (115), and W M'Donald, Warrington. (130). The two ran together for 200 yards, and a supreme effort landed Esstwood a winner by six inches in 4min. 24?-: cc. E Cook, of Widnes (112). came in third, being :five yards behind McDonald. The prizes were : First, marble steile'ng clock and bronze ornaments ; second, six cup silver- plated egg frame ; third, silver-pleed celery dish. NINE STONE BOXING COMPETITION. There were 13 entries in the boxing competition but only three were eligible, the other entrants being over- weight. In the first round F Sweeney, of Warrington, boxed F Thompson of Warrington. The former, adopted his usual " rushing " style and, to use a sporting ex- pression the " claret was tapped " very frequently. Thompson seemed to have he beet of mattes towards the close and was declared winner. Joseph Fairclough, or St. Helens, was allowed a byes in the first round and met Thompson in the final, the result being a victory for Thompson, The first prize was a solid silver cup and the second a silver lever watch.

THAT HOPE DEFERRED MAKETH THE HEART SICK is just as true now as ever it was will be attested by all whose most cherished aspirations Imre remained unfulfilled. In every walk of life we encounter this hankering after the (sunposed) unattainable, whilst in many eases the remedy is close at hand if those interested only knew how to aviil themselves of it. It affects most businesses, the furnishing trade especicily. For instanee, a young man meets a maiden fair whose appearance and merits he approves. She, likewise, appreciates his qualities, and quickly an affection springs up between them. How pleasant they think it would be to marry and start housekeeping together. Then the stumbling block presents itself--where is the cash to purchase furniture to come from ? With hire, time past, like with most young fellows, "enough for the day has been the evil thereof." He has save I practically nothing so the marriage is postponed indefinitely. Now, this is where PITTS S step in with a timely suggestion. TRII COMitITTBH.
The answer of thePosr- Post Office Perform- ances and Puzzles. MASTER-GENERAL to Mr

HENNIKER HEATON'S re- cent long bill of indictment would probably be to present him with a copy of the bulky annual re- port of the Department—certainly one of the most marvellous Blue-books published by the Government. The POSTMASTER-GENERAL almost overpowers us with his stapstics. There is only one thing with which we can compare them ; that is, with the awe-inspiring figures of a work on as tronorny giving the distances of the fixed stars, whose parallax has been ascertained. True, the PosrmAsTicia-GENERAL,,has not yet got into billions in the number of the postal packets he carries for

his nation. But he has reached thousands of mil- lions ; and they produce about the same awe- inspiring and mystifying eflect on the mind as the astronomer's billions. When we learn that 2,246,500,000 letters, 400,300,000 post-cards, 702,800,000 book packets, 163,400,000 news- papers, and 75,418,000 parcels, making a total of 3,588,743,000 postal pockets, wore carried during the year, we can only exclaim,with DOMINIE SAMPSON: " Pro-dee-geous !" The Post Office assuredly shews progress, but Mr. HENNIKER HEATON will, we opine, not be convinced even by its tables of startling statistics that everything is conducted for the best in this marvellous Depart- ment. There are some achievements of the Post Office that are little short of the miraculous. But Londoners only know too well from a recent ex- perience, from which they are still suffering, that it takes very little to throw Post Office machinery out of gear and reduce the postal organisation to chaos. The war in South Africa appears to have done this very effectively. There have been some- thing like twenty-one and a-half millions of letters, post-cards, &c., undelivered during the year; and of these nearly half-a-million were returned from abroad, largely in consequence of the war in South Africa. Some 35,448 letters, &c., addressed to the Transvaal and the Orange Free State, were stopped at Capetwn at the outbreak of the war. But why? Would it not have been a kindly action, and uo disadvantage to ourselves, to have ' handed these over to the Postal Departments of the two States? The Boers would probably have reciprocated. War between nations should not altogethei atop intercourse between relations and personal friends. It is also unsatisfactory to learn that undelivered correspondence in large quantites is still being returned from South jAfrica. Many d3fects of Post Office administration may be picked out of this report, notwithstanding its surprising record. But all the blame for delays, letters going astray, articles lost, and other short- comings of that sort, must not be laid at the door of the POSTMASTER-GENERAL. No fewer than 288,657 postal packets without addresses were posted during the year, and these contained up- wards of £lO,OOO in cash, notes, cheques, &c. The carelessness of the ordinary commercial clerk is sometimes costly. Altogether £726,613, or nearly three-quarters of a million worth of property was found in packages unaddressed or insufficiently addressed, and not delivered on that account What becomes of all this, or of such portion of it as never finds an owner? Does it add a not un- important item to the profits of the Department ? These profits were less last year than the year be- fore. But they still reach three and a quarter millions—amply sufficient to defray the cost of all Mr. HENNrKER HEATON'S projects, and still leave a goodly surplus. But why should the loss on the Telegraph Department be increasing? With over ninety millions of messages passing over the Post Office wires last year, there was an increased defici of £66,569, and the total deficit last year on the Telegraphs, including interest on purchase-money was considerably over half-a-million. Private companies doing much smaller business could make a profit out of telegrapby ; why cannot a Govern- ment Department having a monopoly of the whole inland telegraph business of the country? This is one of the numerous puzzles of the Post Office.

The attempts which are made on the lives of Royal personages may be the outcome of organised Anarchial movements, but they are due, in their inception, to a fanatical craving for importance among the men who promote them. No Anarchist could sustain the argument that any act of his promoted the cause of Socialism, with which he claims to be associated. On the contrary, it gains adherents to existing systems of government among classes who have no enthusiasm at ordinary times for rulers. The fact is so transparent as to make apparent a vanity which mistakes notorieuy for fame. The Italian Government has done wisely in refusing to allow the portrait of Bresci to be published. It is also in the interests of the law-abiding community that the story of Bresci's attitude in prison should be allowed to transpire. Already he is broken in spirit, and his braggart manner is forsaking him. The penalty for regicide in Italy includes a long period of solitary confinement under the most de- pressing conditions, which is worse even than the dreadful scaffold in Great Britain. The judgment at the trial to be held in Italy is a foregone min- elusion, and the misery of this living death is being impressed by the descriptions in the papers. They will act as a healthy corrective in morbid minds to the accounts of the tragedy in which Bresci appeared for a few brief moments on the public stage as the villain of the piece. The thought that his name is to be handed down to posterity as affecting history is a poor consolation even to such a disaffected mind as Bresci's, in the gloom of the prison vault, and any companions who played upon his distorted emotions to the committal of such a crime must read the record with qualms of remorse quickening their enfeebled consciences. It must fill them with regret, and cannot but be a deterrent against similar exploits.

On reading the high prices which have been fetched at open auction by specimens of the Male- king stamps, some of those who passed through the unique experiences of the long siege must be regret- ting their want of foresight. When a set of stamps, the face value of which hardly exceeded a schoolboy's weekly pocket-money, finds a pur- chaser at £39 18s., it is evident that, for the expen- diture of a very few shillings, it would have been pass!' le to secure the making of a small fortune. If oely he could have realised the opportunities which the attack of the Boers was putting in his way many a man in Mafeking might have found Llulately a more profital4le undertaking than gold-mining. It is a high price to pay for a few now absolutely useless rectangular pieces of adhesive paper, and yet those competent to judge of the taste of the people who call themselves philatelists say: that the gentleman who paid down the thirty-eight guineas made an excellent bargain, and will be able in a short time himself to clear a considerable profit on the trans- action. So much prized are these productions of the Maf eking Post office that already a large num- ber of forged specimens have been put about,calling for considerable skill on the part of the expert to distinguish them from the genuine article. The Mafeking stamps will, it is considered, always have historical interest and will, therefore, carry a permanent monetary value. The ways of philate- lists, it is true, are not always clear. The most valuable stamps are not always the rarest. A new fashion may come in at any moment. Purchasers with £39 18s to spare for a few stamps may grow rarer than the sots in the market. Philately, even, may give way to a now craze. For the present, however, the owner of Mafeking stamps appears to have a valuable and improving property.

The Chief Constable's annual report relative to the business of the Brewster Sessions is always an interesting document, and usually contains some very suggestive figures. During the year there were only 302 charges of drunkenness heard by the Warrington Borough bench, as compared with 418 in the preceding twelve months. This is a striking decrease and seems to point to the fact that War- rington is rapidly becoming one of the soberest towns in the kingdom. But we are afraid that the figures are delusive when taken as a gauge of the town's drinking habits. Of the 302 charges which were heard we aro told that 43 of them represent only 15 individuals so that it may be assumed that only 274 different persons appeared before the magistrates. Taking the total as it stands we only get an average of about

MR. LABOUCHERE was Mr Labouchere and one of the members of Mr. Chamberlain. Parliament pointed out by Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, in the somewhat sensa- tional statement made in Parliament as to com- promising correspondence with English M.P.'s having been found at Pretoria. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN has sent Mr. LABOUCHERE a copy of a letter from Mr. MONTAGU WHITE, Transvaal representative in London, to Mr. REITZ, the Transvaal State Secre- tary, and two letters from Mr. LABOUCHERE to Mr. WHITE, asking for his explanation and obser- vations respecting them. Mr. LABOUCFIERE has relieved Mr. CHAMBERLIAN trona all responsibility by publishing the letters himself, with a communi- cation written to Mr. CHAMBERLAIN about them. The member for Northampton does not know "what earthly reason" he Colonial Secretary had to ask members of Parlhament to furnish him with explanations of their letters, and he describes the request as impudence of which no other Minister has been guilty. "To you," says Mr. LABOUCHERE, writing to Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, "I Owe no sort of explanation." All the same, he asks, as a sort of quip modest, if the right hon. gentleman has any explanations or observations to make with regard to his action. In a dialectical encounter cf this sort, Mr. LABOUCHERE probably has the best of it. He has a trained pen, and can use it with rapier-like thrusts. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN is a clumsy controversialist, and lacks the necessary temper to enable him to shine in a literary duel of polished wits. But, at the same time, it can hardly be said that Mr. LABOUCHERE Comes entirely free from blame out of the correspondence. Consider- ing that the Transvaal and this country were at the time the letters passed engaged in delicate negotiations, there are expressions and sentences in his letters to the Transvaal representative which must be characterised as offensive and objection- able. Probably Mr. LABOUCHERE never has had any desire to pose as an English patriot. His sympathies are cosmopolitan. But he is an English member of Parliament, and to tell the represen- tative of a foreign Government that by a " little skilful management" his master "will give Master JOE another fall," or to recommend dilatory tactics with reference to a proposed Joint Commission, and suggest means by which its objects might be defeated (for that we take to be the meaning of the letter to "Dear Mr. WHITE of August 4th, 1899), was hardly consistent with his position, nor was it the way to promote the peace which Mr. LABOUCHERE professed to have in view. The tone of the letters is disloyal and in distinctly bad taste for such a stickler for political etiquette as Mr. LABoucffEnE professes to be. On the other hand, a good deal that the hon. member says in the homily he reads Mr. CHAMBERLAIN is both called for and very P111:11 to the point. Especially in the appeal to him to make a clean breast of the Chamberlain-Hawksley correspondence does Mr. LABOCCHERE score off his antagonist. After the course taken by the right hon. gentleman with reference to these trum- pery letters of English members of Parliament, it is difficult to see how he can refrain from publish- ing what are generally regarded as compromising letters of his own. If there is to be this launder- ing of soiled linen in the eyes of the public, let the contents of the closets on both sides be produced. Mr. LABOUCHERE has himself turned out his own, and his example ought now to be followed by Mr. CHAMBERLAIN. The public confidence in the right hon. gentleman's attitude towards the Raid will never be restored while he keeps back what is known as the Chamberlain-llawksley correspond-

six drunken persons per week all the year ro-ind. Few, who have observed Warrington streets after "closing time" on any week night or on a Saturda!! night when, according to the statement of Alder- man Fairclough, the main streets are "a perfect hell," will be prepared to avow that half a dozen drunken cases a week is a fair :average for War- rington. We have no desire to paint Warrington blacker than it really is but it is quite another thing to persistently use whitewash and blink at facts.

In'the belief that "constant dropping will wear away a stone" we echo the sentiments of Mr. F. Monks expressed in another column with regard to the bad state of many of our streets and roads.Thero cannot be too much re-iteration of the complaints anent this subject for the magnitude of the evil is indeed a scandal and the remedying of it is slower than the progress of the proverbial tortoise. Mr. Monks specifies Liverpool-road and Walton New - road, both of which are bad enough to fret the temper of their users, and other people can just as easily specify thoroughfares even worse in their own neighbourhood. Happily something is con- stantly being done to improve matters, but the progress in one quarter is so slow that the condition of things elsewhere worsens at an extra-proportionate rate. It is the rate of pro- gress which most urgently needs the application of a spur. Wilderspool Causeway will soon be a bright example of what can be done, and with re- gard to it we have a suggestion to respectfully offer. The tarred macadam which was so smoothly laid down the centre is fast becoming cut up by heavy vehicular traffic. Why not, therefore, com- pel all horse-vehicles to keep to the set-paved portions of the broad road and leave the centre for the illused cyclist. He had hardly begun to rejoice ere the surface alluded to began spoiled by vehicles which have no need to use whatever. By this means the Corporation might save expense, and benefit a considerable portion of the community at the same time, without even in conveniencing traffic.

The Borough Treasurer's Abstract of Accounts, which has just been issued, is a bulky tome of some 180 pages. Its issue at this time of the year can hardly be said to be timely for it is searcelY volume which the average ratepayer would care to include amongst his literature for seaside reading. Nevertheless it contains some interesting facts. If the ratepayer has a notion that the Corporation is a very extra- vagant body he will probably find certain Awns in the accounts which will confirm him in hie opinion. It all depends upon the point of view, A mere outsider may feel convinced that deputa- tions to London, Blackpool and Southampton are disguised holidays at the ratepayers' expense, but such an opinion will not be held by t 1100.6 who participated in them; in fact it is probable that the outsider would be told that the deputations were of great value to the Corpora- tion. It may also come as a mild shock to the sorely-oppressed ratepayer to find it stated in cold type that the cost of the Corporation Bill in the 1899 session of Parliament was £6,860 2s lid. It is some consolation to find that the Corporatiol:l makes money as well as snends it. The Gas el' Water Works and Markets show handsome profits on the year's working, and it is also SatiS' factory to see that the Parr Hall has made a egir stantial profit for the first time. The balanc'e hand after meeting the year's expenses of the hali,l9 £172 13s 11d.The whole of the accounts are clearl set forth, and the improvement, which has beell noticeable in the presentation of recent Corp°re. tion statements of accounts is well maintained.
