div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

Many people in the provinces are at the present Moment seriously discussing the prospects of a long and bard winter. Meteorology being as yet a somewhat inexact science, no one can safely say What kind of weather there will be, but, be it what it may, tbe increased cost of many necessaries of life is looked forward to as a certainty. The greatly increased price of coal affects, more or less, and directly or indirectly, the price of almost everything else, particularly articles in the production of Which coal is a factor. Foodstuffs and clothing have for some weeks past shown an upward tendency, and, as experience has taught, when there is an advance in one direction the same invariably happens in others. Dearness, like "con- fiscation. 'to borrow a Disraelian saying, "is con- tagions," and the coal crisis has raised an Imperial as well as a domestic question. The proposed in- clusion of fuel among the things which may be pro- hibited from exportation in the event of war,would not altogether meet the case of the Navy. Action ought to be taken beforehand, and if the canons of Free Trade are eternal and unalterable,as sometimes represented, the Government should acquire mines of the right kind and work them independently of all others.

That is to say, the mines should be worked solely with a view to the requirements of the fleet. It Would be a difficult matter to suggest a really practical remedy of which the hard-pinched householder could readily avail himself. No doubt both gas and oil will be more generally used next Winter than last, at an increased cost, and mean- While we may continue to hear a good deal of the probable use of "rich bog peat." But whether it will be extensively used is another question. Fuel in this. form is not likely to supersede coal in the average English household. Yet, under the pressure 9f scarcity and high prices, the primitive peat, cut Into blocks, may at no distant date become an article of commerce in general demand.

There has been either yet another or a continua- tion of the same reminder, that owing to the with- drawal of so many men from the ordinary occupa- tions to join the ranks of the Army Reserve, Royal Reserve, and Militia, farmers are terribly short- handed for harvest work. In consequence of these complaints,a special furlough of a month's duration has been granted to reservists and militiamen desir- ous of going home for harvesting,and it has proved an excellent step so far as the men themselves and the farming classes are concerned. The fact that it should be necessary, however, illustrates the diffi- culty of combining the principles of voluntary and Compulsory service, which is what our present System does") soon as military requirements begin seriously to effect the numbers of the male popu- lation available for civil occupations. Notwith- Standing all the discussion that has recently taken place, and despite the large amount of gratuitous advice tendered to the War Office, the country still awaits a more perfect system of national defence.

Anent the excess luggage question, the public are anxiously anticipating the action or intention c,f other companies, since the Midland Railway Company gave notice that from an early date the amount of free luggage allowed would be 1001bs. third-class, and 1401135. for first-class passengers.
A BEGGAR DISPOSED OF AT RUNCORN.

John Rigby, describing himself as a spinner, of Preston, pleaded guilty to begging from house to house in Duke-street, Runcorn,when charged before Messrs. IT Norman and S Taylor, at the Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday.—The case was proved by P.C. It Gilpin.—Prisoner was sentenced to seven days hard labour. MERSEY MISSION TO SEAMEN, RUNCORN.

On Sunday, anniversary services were celebrated in the above mission. Mr: Joseph Stokes, Rock Savage, preached to a large congregation in the morning, whilst in the evening the pulpit was occupied by Mr J. W. Davies, Farnworth. A children's service was held in the afternoon, when Mr J. W. Davies preached. Special musical items were rendered by the choir and children. The col- lections were satisfactory. BETHESDA CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH, RUNCORN The annual choir sermons in connection with the above church were preached on Sunday by the Rev J. Osborne. The musical portion of the services was an excellent feature. in the morning the choir gave a capital rendition of the anthem" Arise, shine" (Elvey), whilst the items" It is high time to awake "(Barnby) and "Seek ye the Lord" (Roberts) received admirable treatment in the evening. Miss P. Humphreys (pupil of Mr W. H. Griffiths) gave a very choice interpretation of the solos " Les Rameaux " (J. Faure) and "The Holy City " (S. Adams) at the evening service. The collections were on behalf of the choir fund. PRIZE DISTRIBUTION AT NELSON-STREET SUNDAY SCHOOL.

Mr. F J Norman, on Sunday afternoon last, at- tended the Nelson-street Sunday School and distri- buted prizes to about one hundred children for their regularity and diligence at the schools. Mr Norman pressed upon the recipients the course they received the prizes for, and hoped thair success would emu- late the other scholars to follow in their steps. Afterwards the scholars rendered a service of song entitled " Our Joe," an,4 their singing of the hymns was especially creditable.—ln the evening a flower service was held when Mr R H Posnett was the preacher. Retaining a flower in his hand the preacher drew a beautiful lesson from the plant.— Both services were largely attended and the collec- tions were devoted to the prize fund. SUPPOSED ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT RUNCORN. About 5.30 on Thursday morning Thomas Fax, a dock labourer, of 17, Fryer-street, was found in his bedroom with his throat cut in a very serious manner. It appears that a man named Mulhearn found the deceased upon the bedroom floor bleeding profusely from a knife wound in the throat. Fax's son who slept with him was at that time fast asleep; Dr Delaney was summoned and at once attended to the injured man. The wound was fully an inch deep and though no important arteries were severed the loss of blood and inflammation that the man subsequently suffered from has caused him to become comatose and he now lies in a very critical condition. It is supposed that he attempted to commit suicide, by cutting his throat with a pen- knife.

div.head: ASSAULTING THE WIDNES POLICE.
div.p: ASSAULTING THE WIDNES POLICE.

At the Widnes Police Court,on Monday,before the Mayor (Alderman G. I. Niel) and Alderman Ware- ing, John Rigby, Midwool-street, was charged with being drunk and disorderly and assaulting P.C: Davidson and Inspector Strickland ; also with damaging a cell to the extent of 73 61.—P.0. David- son stated that he found the prisoner drunk at one o'clock on Sunday morning. Upon requesting him to go home prisoner refused, and threw himself to the ground Persuasive measures being unavailing, the prisoner was brought to the Police Station. He used bad language, and on Inspector Strickland coming upon the scene he became very violent. Witness was struck on the jaw and kicked, and the Inspector also received several kicks about the legs —P.C. Evans spoke to seeing the prisoner damaging the cell. When asked why he had done it he replied" For satisfaction for being locked up."— Prisoner was fined 23 6d and costs for being drunk, lOs and costs on each of the charges of assault, and is and 7s 6d costs for the damage to the cell, mak- ing a total of £2 3s, or one month's imprisonment. (Prisoner went to gaol.)

div.head: SAILOR THIEF AT RUNCORN.
div.p: A SAILOR THIEF AT RUNCORN.

At Runcorn Police Court, on Tuesday, Magnus Gear, a sailor of the Shetland Islands, was charged with stealing from the schooner Constance.of Inver- ness, a pair of marine binoculars, value £1 54. The evidence showed that the prisoner was a seaman on the vessel, and was paid off at Runcorn on Friday. On Saturday the captain, Edward Master Williams, went to his home at Portdinorwic. On returning to Runcorn on Monday the captain found his cabin had been broken into and the binoculars taken. Suspicion fell upon the prisoner, and in the evening, from the description he had received, Detective-sergeant Gregory appre- hended the prisoner in High-street and took him to the police station. Prisoner denied all knowledge of the glasses, and was highly indignant that he should be suspected, and threatened to bring an action both against the detective and the captain of the ship. Prisoner promised to remain in Runcorn, at the Sailors' Home until the glasses were found, and Detective Gregory set him at liberty, but shadowad him. The prisoner went straight to the railway station and inquired the time of the next train to Garstont and Detective Gregory promptly telephoned to the police there, with the result that the glasses were found pawned with Mr. Johnson of King-street. Detective Gregory there again ap- prehended the prisoner who confessed his guilt and exoressed sorrow. The prisoner was sentenced to 14 days' bard labour.
FUNERAL OF THE LATE Mn. JOSEPH EDWARDSON,
WIDNI39.

The remains of the late Mr. Joseph Edwardson,of Widnes, were interred in Farnworth Parish Church- yard on Saturday afternoon. Deceased had had a somewhat remarkable experience in the army. He was 71 years of age, and for 21 years was associated with the 31st East Surrey Infantry. He had gone through the Crimean war and was present at the siege of Sebastopol. He was also in the Kaffir war, the In&an mutiny, and the Chinese rebellion of 1860, receiving a medal with bar for Sebastopol, a Turkish medal with bar for the Crimean campaign, and a medal for the taking of the Taku Forts in China. Re also assisted in the quelling of the Fenian rising at the end of the forties. The funeral procession on Saturday started from Appleton, near Warrington, where deceased had resided, those pre- sent including Messrs John, William, Frederick,and Arthur Edwardson (sons), Mr and Mrs Hayward (son and daughter), Mr William Edwardson (brother), Mr James Edwardt,on (cousin),,...lrs Jos. Edwardson (daughter-in-law), and Mrs StriCkliand. The last rites were performed by the Itev. W. Thatcher. Wreaths were sent by the following :--; Mr and Mrs Dean (Applet3n, Warrington), Mr and Mrs Hayward (Warrington), Widnes postmen, Mr and Mrs Strickland, Mr and Mrs William Edward- son,Mrs Joseph Edwardson,and Mr Arthur Edward- son. Mr James Hayward, of Warrington, was the undertaker, and Mr 3 Woods, Widnes, supplied the coaches.

RUNCORN CO OPERATIVE SOCIETY'S EXCURSION. The annual excursion in connection with the Runcorn Co-operative Society took place on Monday the rendezroug this year being Morecambe. The weather outlook was anything but promising at Runcorn at the time of departure. There had been a heavy rainfall overnight and in the early hours, and the face of the sky was not very encouraging to holiday seekers. These conditions, however,did not deter a large proportion of Runcornians from availing themselves of a cheap outing to the seaside and between 300 and 400 boarded the special train which left the station shortly after 6.30. Stop- pages were made at Ditton, Appleton, and Farn- worth to pick up members belonging to the Widnes and district, branches of the society, together with other friends, and the train was at length filled to its utmost capacity. Good running was made, and the trippers arrived at their des- tination shortly after nine o'clock. After attending to the wants of the inner man the visitors scattered themselves over the town and neighbour- hood, a large number finding healthful pleasure from a sail round the lightship in the bay, others devoting their energie,, to angling in the briny waters, and some preferring a drive through the charming scenery in the adjacent countryside. The visi`ors were delighted to fine Old Sol beaming down upon them as they were happily favoured with a continuance of his genial influence almost throughout the whole day. In the afternoon the Winter Gardens, Pier, and other attractions of the town were liberally patronizA, and when the tiip- pers returned to the station at 6 p.m. to start upon the homeward journey they were all agreed that the day's outing had been of the most enjoyable character. Runcorn was reached about 9.30 p.m. The arrangements of the committee gave general satisfaction.

div.head: EXAMINER, 14RMAY, AUGUST 24, 1900.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, 14RMAY, AUGUST 24, 1900.

SUCCESSFUL RUNCORN AND WIDNES ATHLETES. At the National Cycle Union meeting at Rock Ferry, II W hid, of Runcorn, came second in the half mile bicycle centre championship. Second place in the 120 yards flat race at the Lyme Horti- cultural Society gatherinz, was gained by J Ingles- field, Runcorn, with 10i yards start. At the same meeting J Egan, Farnworth, with 130 yards, won the mile flat race very easily.—E Cook, Widnes, ran third in the mile flat race, with 112 yards, at the Warrington Football Club Sports. At the Crompton Cricket and Bowling Club sports G Wright, Wid- nes, with 54 yards, obtained the second place in the half mile flat race. CHELL PLAYS A NEW' ROLE AT RNNCORN.

Only as late as Saturday, Frederick Coell, (a well- known character) was delivered from a term of imprisonment at Knutsford,and arrived in Runcorn. Tuesday, however, saw him in the hands of the police, and on Wednesday morning Messrs. If J Nor- man ann S Taylor sat to adjudicate upon charges of begging and using obscene language, which was preferred against bim by Constable Brett. From the evidence of the Constable and Mrs Mary Shallcross (who keeps a confectioner's shop near the theatre), it appears that Frederick ' went to the shop at about 9-30 in the morning, in quite a frolicksome mood. He asked for lid, but was refused, consequent upon which he became both violent and abusive, and terrified Mrs. Shall- cross and her daughter so much that they left the shop. Chell than took possession, and at once began to assure everyone who approached the place that he was a captain or King or some other great potentate. The news of the occurrence reaching Constable Bratt he went there and quickly assured Chell that he was no other than _Frederick Chell, greengrocer, of Runcorn, a character well-known to the whole police force,and it was not long afterwards that poor Chell found himself under lock and key.—The Bench deci- ded to commit Chell for one month with hard labour. —Prisoner said that he would go to his relations in Staffordshire if he was let off. The Chairman: Well, you will be nearer to Staffordshire when you leave Knutsford.—Prisoner : Yes. But my bargain is to go if you let me off.—The Chairman said it was undoubtedly beer that made the prisoner act as he did, and it was a great mistake on his part to take any. As it was he would have to be taught to behave himself and could not be allowed to go about terrifying people. He would have to go to prison as stated,and the other charge would be withdrawn.-- Prisoner made a rambling statement,in which he laid claim to being a preacher at St. Paul's Church, and was a better man at the game than his grandfather was. Then branching off he claimed to be King of Kings, and the surveyor to the Urban District Council, as well as quite a respectable honest gen- tleman. His removal ended his discourse.—Super- intendent Pearson stated that prisoner since his discharge from prison had locked himself in a stable and altogether acted remarkably.

LICENSING SESSIONS, Six New Applications defused. More than usual interest was taken in the pro- ceediegs at the Warrington Borough Police Court on Thursday, when the general annual licensing meeting "for granting and renewing alehouse, music and dancing,and other licenses," was held. There were on the Bench the Mayor (Alderman Roberts), Colonel Ridgway, Messrs. Monks, Chand- ley, Birchen, Pierpoint, Geddes, Guest, Francomb, Sutton, Hayward, Hepherd. The Licensing Com- mittee consists of the Mayor (Alderman Roberts), and Messrs. Birchen, Ridgway, Piercoint, Geddes, Monks, and E J Guest. There was a large attend- ance of the general public at the back of the Court. Amongst those present we noticed Councillor Plumpton, Councillor Peacock, Mr William Roberts, Mr F A Jenkins, Mr Drury and other temperance advocates as well as a large number of persons interested in " the trade." Mr. Overend Evans (instructed by Mr. Willett), represeiated. Mr Thomas Hardman and Hannah Walker; Mr Rigby Swift (instructed by Messrs. Buckton and Greenall), appeared on behalf of two other applicants for licenses.—Mr William Wych and Councillor Peaceck: Mr Arthur Browne represented Mr. Benjamin Kenyon and Mr. William Davies, whilst Mr. Steel opposed the appli- cations on behalf of residents. THE CHIEF CONSTABLE'S REPORT. The Chief 4i7,old'i naloal reput watch was sub mitted to the justices read as follows :—" Gentlemen,— I have the honour to submit to you my fifth annual report relative to the business of the Brewster &osiong, tn period dealt with being the year ended July 31st, 1900. Subsequent to the last .extension of the borough bliandaries the population, according to the census of 1891, was 55,063. P was now compu-ed at 61,000. Tiivre are in the town 87 alehouoes,39 bserhouses.and 85 " off-licensed "premises (including those licensed for the sale of wine or spirits), total 211, a proportion of one license to every 312 79 of the estimated population. One be.erhouse-keeper was summoned for serving constables on duty with beer, and the case was dis- missed on payment of costs. Over six hundred visits of supervision have been paid to licensed premises by ' inspectors and serge nts detailed for such duty, and 20 Licence holders have been cautioned by these officers for irregularities not amounting to actual breaches of the licensing law. The licensed 'houses, on the whole, have been well conducted. Licences have been transferred to eight licensed victuallers, three beerhouse-keepers, and 14 off-licence holders, making a total Rf 25 transfers, the same number as during last year. Twenty-six alehouses, sir beernouses, and twelve other public rlJrno are licensed for music and dancing. At the a!ehouses and beerhenses so licensed NO professional performers are employed. For the performance of stage plays ten places are licensed. During the year the magistrates have dealt with 302 charges of drunkeeness, viz :-202 against male perseas and 103 against fema!ee. There were 273 convictions and 29 persons were cautioned au-I dismissed. Last year the charges oh drankenness were 418, or 116 in excess of this year's total. Of the persons charged during the present year, 203 v7re residents of the town, and 94 were persons who (sad no permanent abode here. I should point out that one person was c)victed six times, on four times, seven thr-e times, and six persons twice during the year, so that 43 of the charges repre- sent only 15 individuals. There is as yet no provision in this locality in the shape of a home for inebriates under the Inebriates Act of 1393, but such a much- needed institution is, I understand, to be provided, as early as practicable, by the jo'nt action of the County ani Borough Authorities of Lancashire. The name of the Groat Central Hotel, Win wick-street, was altered to the Midland Hotel, by permission of justices, on Septem- ber 29th. The Howley Hotel wss formally opened on February 26th, in consideration of welch the liceaces of the Crow alehouse, Bridge-street, the Rose beerhouse, Dial-street, and the off-license at 51, Gerd Nelson-street, were allowed to lapse. Accompanying the report is a list shoe-leg the num- ber of houses, of licensing prosecutions and of charges of drunkenness in the brugh &ring each year of the oast decade. In 1891 there ware 88 licensed victuallers: 48 beerhouoes and 73 shopkeepers as compar(d with 87 licensed victuallers, 39 beerhouse keepers and 85 shop- keepers at the present time. In 1831 the charges of drunkenness were 773; 1892, 680 ; 1893, 606 ; 1894,458 ; 1895, 323 ; 1896, 261. ; 1897, 266 1898, 276 ; 1899, 418 ; 1900, 302. A veered table gives a comparative return of the statistics of drunkenness in several other towns and cities, the figures being relltive to the same period dealt with in the report. We extract from it the follow- ing statistics : Total Present Proceeded Estimated Per 1,030 of Against. Populatiol. Population Salford Middlesboro' 774 Barrow-in- Furness York Wakefield 491 ..... 40,0)0 Stockport Oldham Rochdale ...... 325 Huddersfield... 258 Halifax Wigan Bolten Burnley 395 100,000 ..... 3-95 Blackburn Birkenhead ... 934 Preston Bootle Hanley Warrington ... 302 LICENSE HOLDERS CAUTIONED BY THE BENCH. Tao Mayor said he would like, before the business commenced, to call attention to the remark in the Chief Constable's report in reference to the 20 license-holders who had been cautioned by the Inspector and Sergeant detailed for the special duty in regard to irregularities which did not amount to actual breaches of the licens- ing laws. The Bench did not propose to take any notice of them that morning beyond stating that they were assured by the Chief Constable that in most cases these irregularities had not been serious, but the magistrates thought it their duty to give notice Viet next year it ml :ht be necessary to ask the Chief Cen- stabie to furnish the Bench with a list of all names of licensees in whose houses irregularities had been corn- mitted, and they would be talvn into consideration in I, regard to the applications for renewals. ALEHOUSE AND BEERHOUSE LICENCES. No objection was raised, and the alehouse and beer- house licences were renewed. RENEWAL OF OFF-LICENSES. THE LONG PULL TO BE DISCONTINUED. • There was no objection to the renewal of the off- licenses. The Mayor said with regard to these applications the Bench had reason to believe that 60 far as a number of off-licensee were concerned, what was known as the long pull was in existence,and he was authorized to say on behalf of his colleagues that it was probabj,ethey would ask the Chief Constable to furoislithe ext with a list of such off-teerhouse lieetisei as persisted in giving the long pull. They hoped ,the long pull would be discontinued after these suggestions from the Bench. If it were not, it might be necessary for the Bench to take into consideration the fact that it had not been dis- continued in regard to the applications made for re- newals next year. Personally he should be very glad if this suggestion were carried out loyally by off-beerhouse licensees. Mr. Browne asked if what was meant was giving more than the regulation wed stipulated measure? The Mayor thought it was well understood what the long pull was. They wished it to be discontinued. Mr. Browne observed that it differed in certain places. The Mayor : We want it discontinued as it is in War- rington. The Chief Constable remarked that anything above the measure was a long pull. Mr. Browne: Does that apply to fully licensed houses ? Tae Mayor : We have no knowledge of its existence there. We hope our suggestion will be carried out in regard to those if necessary. The Chief Constable said the long pull was pretty com- mon in all houses, fully licensed and otherwise. The Mayor stated that the application of William Shaw Carmichael, of Priory-buildings, Bridge-street, would be adjourned until the 28th of Sept enber,in order that he might satisfy the Bench that he WAS the keeper of a shop within the meaning of the Act of Parliament. The other licenses would be renewed. BILLIARD LICENCE FOR THE CAFE. Mr. Willett applied on behalf of Mr. William Roberts for a billiard licence for Cie Winmarleigh Calf:, 70, Sankey-street. Mr. Roberts, who is the secretary of the Warrington ('aids, Limited, said that there was no other building in Warringion holding a licence of this description where intoxicating liquors were not sold. A number of cus- tomers had asked bim to obtain a billiard licence. There was no objection, acid the licence WAS granted. PROPOSAL TO RE-BUILD THE WHEAT SHEAF. MAGISTRATES TO INSPECT THE PLACE. Mr. Browne applied for permission for the re-building of the Wheat Sheaf, off Pinner's-brow. He said the real I ground of the application was that the domestic accom- modation was absolutely inadequate, practically amount- ing to only three rooms. It was proposed to re-build the house on exactly the same ground and to take in seme cottages for enlarging the yard and providing conveniences there. The matter was brought before the Watch Committee some few months ago, and it was then thoueht by the committee that it was a matter they ought net to recommend the magistrates to grant, but that it should go before the Bench as a whole. He put in plans prepared by the late Mr Alderman Wright which showed tbo alterations proposed to be made. The drinking area of the house was not increased. Mr Monks : It means the conversion of a third rate public-house into a first-rate one.

Mr. Browne said that was not so. This was a very good house for licensing purposes, but the domestic ac- commodation was simply terrible. They had no room but the kitchen in which to have their food, and there was not room there to swing a rat round. The sanitary conditions were also bad.
The Mayor mentioned that a shop was taken in the 133 W plan.

Mr. Browne sail the ce:lar of the publichouse went under the shop. The shop was cot tenanted. The Mayor said the Bench had considered the matter and were disposed to visit the premises. Mr. Browu pointed out tuat tile building seas)n was well advanced.
rho Mayor said the place would keep that long. They would visit the premises, and report to the adj3urned sessions.
MUSIC LICENSES.
There nein' no objection, tee rnuic liceaseg were re- newed.
"THE GREEN MAN" BEEREIOUSE. ALEHOUSE LICENSE REFUSED.

Mr. Browne applied on behalf of Benjamin Kenyon.of the" Green Ran " beertiouse, Green-strieet for an ale- house license. He said the application had been made on a number of occasions, and the Bench knew the full particulars regarding the hoase. It would, therefore, be a waste of time to put any witnesses forward. The condition of things at the present time was the same as last year. There was no traerhouse towards Sankey nearer than the Rose, about a mile away, the other way there was none for nearly a mile, the Imperial, along Powya-street,there were the Bowling Green and the Ship Inn, while towards Warrington there was none nearer than the White Hart io Sankey-street. With the excep- tion of the 13.3w1itig, Green and the Ship Inn it was more than bait ra mile- from any other house. Tois was a suitable house for a full license. It was not a tied house, being owned by Mrs. Kenyon, who desired to have a full beerhouse license. The granting of a spirit license, which was practically what was asked for, did not incnerve the value. There were beerhoures in the market fetching quite as much as fully licensed houses' The only reason the application was submitted was because so many requests were made by eustomers for spirits in the house. _ . _

Thl Chief Constable oppaied the application. /t was, be said, refused last year,ancl no new facts were adduced in support ot it. There were three alehouses, a beer- house, and nine off-licenses within four hundred yards. The neighbourhood was populous but it was provided for.

Mr. Browne : A large number of homes have been built round there from year to year. Mr. Steel said he was instructed by a number of resid cuts to oppose the application, but as the circumstances as stated by Mr. Browne were unchanged, be dii not think the magistrates would agree to what their prede- cessors thought unnecessary. As the Chief Cinstable said, the place just about there was swarming with pu'-)lichouses.
The Chief Constable: I did not say swarming. :Laughter.

le !magistrates decided to give their decision after hearing the other applications. BEER WANFED IN SMALL QUAN Mr. Overeni Evans made an application for a bser (off) licence oa behalf of Thomas Lia,rdman, in respect of premises at 67, Longford-street. He pointed out that Mr. Hardman had already a beer- baler's excise licence, but he now applied for an additional licence for the sale of beer to be consumed off the pre- mises. The circumstances that had been operated on the mind of Mr Hardman in making this application were that he found the customers for whom he catered rather disinclined to take so large a quantity as 41 gallons at a time or two dozen reputed quarts in homes. These were the smallest quantities wnich Mr Hardman could supply with the license Le now held. Mr Hardman catered for people in the country and not for the people in the immediate neighbourhood of his own premises. He did not do and did not wish to do a jug business but what he wanted to do was to supply and be in a position to receive orders from people at a distance for smaller quantities than those he was now ins position to suppiy. There was a demand hr stnaler quantities. Mr. Hardman had horses and carts of his own and he was in every way qualified for carrying on a business of this kind. He wished Co be able to supply beer in quantities of not less Ulla a dozen half-pints. and deliver th ‘m on the premises of his Customers. He was quits willing to give an undertak- ing net to sell less titan a doz ea bottles, uot to do any jug business or deliver beer over the couater, but to deliver 'everything at the houses of his customers in pursuance of orders received from them . His customers did not care to resort to the public-houses for their beer but were desirous of obtaining it in a respectable way in small quantities from the applicant, who would deliver it at the houses. Some of Mr Hardman's custom,rs lived a considerable distancn from public-houses and in some cases there wal no possiblity of obtaining it within a distance of three

The Mayor : You are asking us to believe something which i contrary to our knowledge. Mr. Evans said he did not lin )w the district in ities• tion, but he was informed that one of Mr. Hardman's customers was named Clarke, of High La, wad he believed, if his brief were cornet, chit he was at least thr3e miles from a fully licensed house. The Mayor: You surely do not wish us to believe that Mr. Clarke of High Legb is going to be in a better position to obtain drink by means of an off-licensed house in Longford-street. You have got to go through Warrington from one end to the other in order to got to Longford-street from High Legb. Mr. Monks: They will be very dry before they get there. (Laughter.) Mr. Evans said the Bench could question the man when he calm before them. Mr. Hardman was willing to give the undertaking he had mentioned. If the undertaking were not faithfully kept, then the Bench could decide not to renew his licence in the future. THE DECISION OF THE LICENSING COMMITTEE.

Other app!icttions for off-leetises from Mrs. Wa Mr. Davies, Mr. Wych and Mr. Peacock were then pro- ceeded with. At 25 minutes to one the Licensing Com- mittee retired to consider their decision and on their return into court in a few minutes the Mayor announced that the whole of the applicatiens had been unanimously refused.

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES.
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES.
[BY A CORRESPONDENT.]
FOOTBALL.

The Runcorn Football Club have at length settled their little differences, and the turn out at the first of the practice matches on Tuesday evening last was highly satisfactory. Nearly everyone of last year's players of both first and second strings took the field.and displayed a form and vitality gratify- ing in the extreme to the many supporters present. To speculate upon Runcorn's prospects for the com- ing season will be my task for next week, as by that time I shall have obtained a view of the other Northern Union competitors' form, sal will be able to make better comparison. Young Taylor who met his death so tragically whilst boating on tbe Dee some short time ago was missed from the ranks of his fellow-players.

The erection of a much more up-to-date and com- modous stand for the accommodation of spectators has been undertaken by the committee, and will meet a long felt want. The field of play too has undergone necessary re-arrangement and in future it will be able to accommodate thousands more spectators so that should Runcorn be so successful as lasi, year,visitors can come in their hundreds and not only get on to the ground,but also get a view of the game for their money.

The Runcorn Cycle Parade is now a thing of the past, yet, the memory of the pageant will not soon sink into oblivion as one would generally suppose. Throughout the whole town the support accorded has been both generous and enthusiastic and an- other" nugget' has been secured for that laudable object, the Cottage Hospital. The usefulness of a Cottage Hospital in a town like Runcorn cannot be too highly dwelt upon, and the sooner one could see it an accomplished fact the better. Before the parade commenced the total fund stood at .£631 of which £3ll was the result of collections at previous parades ; and £320 the "sound promises of local gentry.' In addition too, there is an encouraging offer from the Manchester Ship Canal Company of £5O per annum towards maintenance for the first three years, provided £l5O is guaranteed from other sources. "Thus it will be seen the project stands within healthy surroundings," and it only remains for all to keep their shoulder to the wheel a few seasons longer to consummate an admirable work, which will bring credit to the town and alle- viate untold sufferings.

The election of a County Councillor for the casual vacancy in Runcorn North, consequent upon the death of Mr. James Handley has resulted in the un- opposed return of Mr A. R. Norman, J.Y., of Linden Lodge, Runcorn, a vice-president of the Runcorn Liberal Club, and a gentleman well-known in the town. At the last County Council election Mr. Norman opposed Mr. E. Imison, C.C., for Runcorn South but was unsuccessful.

His Honour Judge Nforton Smith in his remarks upon the case of Ball v Duckett heard at the Run- corn County Court on Thursday last spoke rather strongly and to the paint upon the horrible misuse of the word" bloody" which it was very evident, from the evidence adduced before him, had been used with great frequency by both parties. " The horrible word "said the learned Judge, "was only too commonly used in the streets of the towns one passed through. Men did not fully understand what it meant and it was a silly, stupid, senseless word to use. He hoped the time would come when people would be ashamed to use the word so in their language. As it was, it was used almost to intersperse every other word by some people." I cordially echo the learned Judge's sentiments. Pro- fanity is always detestable and perhaps a good way of lessening the evil would be to condemn it piece- meal, or word by word.
COUNTY COUNCIL ELECTION FOR RUNCORN•
Unopposed Return of Mr. A. R. Norman.

The election of a representative for the County Coun- cil vacancy, caused by the death of the late Mr. James Handley, of Holly Bani, Ga.rston, in Runcorn north has now been accomplished without a contest. Nominations were received on Wednesday and objec- ti9n9 heard on Thursday by Mr. G. F. Ashton, deputy returning officer, at his offices in High-street. Very little interest was taken in the matter, and the only nomination received was that of Mr. Alfred R. Norman, J.P., of Lindon Lodge, Runcorn. Mr. Norman is a Liberal and a vice-president of the Runcorn Liberal Club a member of the Board of Guardians, and a c.!ontlemn who interests himself in public affairs generally.

Mid-Cheshire Railwaymen's Parade. The railway men of Northwich, Crewe, Warring- ton, Winsford, and other districts joined the North- wich branch of the Amalgamated Society of Rail- way Servants, on Sunday,in an interesting effort on behalf of the orphan fund of that organisation. In the afternoon and evening processions were organ- ised at the Northwich Station, and were joined by many of the leading tradesmen and townspeople of Northwich. The Verdin Adelaide Band led the way, and the railway banner was carriei. In the after- noon a special service was held at Witton Parish Church, the Rev. A Guest (vicar of Peover) being the preacher. At night the Congregational Church was visited, the Rev. J T Miles (pastor) delivering the sermon.

div.head: RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT NEWTON.
div.p: RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT NEWTON.

On Monday night an accident of a peculiar nature occurred at Newton-le Willows Station on the London and North-Western Railway. The train due at Newton at 5.10 p.m., was shifting into the siding to allow the Liverpool empress to pass when the engine cr4shed into the stop blocks, the first car- riage mounting on to the engine and the majority of the train being derailed. Fortunately, the train was empty but for one old lady who had entered it in mistake, and she escaped without injury. The accident happening in the siding, no stoppage of traffic occurred.

div.head: ADVANTAGE AND DISADVANTAGE OF TEETOTALISM.
div.p: THE ADVANTAGE AND DISADVANTAGE OF TEETOTALISM.

Tais was a case in:which Cnarles Ball, fruiterer,High- otreet, Runcorn, sued George Duckett, fruiterer aud fish dealer, of Church-street, Runceria, for damages for assault.—Mr. Pugh, barrister, Liverpool (instructed by Mr. F. A. Lake, solicitor, Ruacorn), appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Jeale, solicitor, Liverpool, for the detendant.—From the evict,: nee of plaintiff it appeared that on Friday, the 13:13 of July, both he and defendant travelled together from Widnes to Liverpool. In the train there were about eight others, Plaintiff and defendant had a conversation about some bet in which plaintiff had acted as referee between Duckett and his son. Then the conversation had turned upon the advantages and disadvantages of teeto-Aism. The upshot was that upon reaching Um s-street Station Duckstt had assaulted Bill by pushing uim against the coaches of the train. The parties then went a little further and Duckett struck Ball a blow with his fist in the neck. A third assault was made upon Ball by Duckett when near the entrance of Lime-street Station. The plaintiff alleged that the result of the assault was tkat he had been suffering since and was only able to partially look after his business.—William A.ckerley,another fruiterer,cf Church-street,corroborated the assault, but in cross-examination said it was a common occurrence for Ball to put out his double-thumb and say "See this ?"—(Laughter.)—)dr. Close,the guard of the train in which the parties travelled, in the employ of the London and North-Western Railway Company, testified to seeing Duckett lift up his arms and push the plaintiff Ball away. Ball staggered and his hat was knocked off.—Dr. A. McLennan, of Runcorn, testified to being called in to see the plaintiff on Monday. He found him suffering from a swel.iug on the right side of the cheek over the lower jaw. There was a slight exercsa of the skin on the back part of the neck and both the lips were cut on the inside. The wounds were such that would be caused by a man's fist. Plaintiff was also nervous and his hearing was slightly affected. George Duckett ,the defendant, contradic:ed the whole of the allegations, and alleged that Ball had Con- tinually aggravated him and wanted him to hit him so that he could summon him for it. He never once struck Ball, but admitted pushing him away twice, once in the station and once outside.—John Hall, Widnes, said he was with the parties all the time, and would think that one was as bad as the other. They were continually falling out. Duckett never struck Ball a deliberate blow. —John Growcott, butcher, Widnes, corroborated the fact that Ball had threatened Duckett with his thumb consequent upon some cooversation regarding the merits or demerits of teetots.l- - Witness had not seen any deliberate blows struck —George C. Duckett, son of the defendant, was called. —His Honour said be hoped that the case would be some good in getting the father and son upon good terms after an estrangement of three years.—Witness proceed- ing said upon getting out of the station Bill kept going close up to him and seemed to be aggravating his fathers He was sure that Mr. Ball shaved himself to- wards his father, and his father asked him to go away or he would strike him.—James McLeary, wholesa'e fruiZerer,Widnes, said according to his opinion he would think that Ball was the aggressor and not Duekettt— James Bennett, copper sampler, Widnes, was also of opinion that Ball and not Duckett was the ageressor— His Honour in summing up said it was for the jury to decide whether any assault had been committed, or whether Duckett had simply acted within his rioht3 and only used sufficient violence to protect himself ? If an assault had been committed they would als) assess the amount of damages.—The jury found for the plaintiff and awarded 103 damages, and 30s doctor's fees, with costs.

div.head: " QUEEN OF SHEBAH" GOLD PAINT
div.p: THE " QUEEN OF SHEBAH" GOLD PAINT
AND THE PAINTER.

This was an action which Messrs. Thomas Coppick and Co. gold paint and varnish manufacturers of Stock- port, Manchester, brought against Mr. J Paynter, of Church-street, Runcorn, painter and decorator for the recovery of £2O lie for goods sold and delivered.—Mr. Saul, barrister, (instructed by Mr: F war, solicitor, Manchester), appeared for the plaintiff ; and Mr Pugh, barrister, Liverpool (instructed by Mr. J Burton, solici- tor), Runcorn, for the defence.—John William Betts,said he was a traveller for Messrs Coppock. He was in RuncJrn on the seti of December, and told defendant he represented Messrs Coppock and Co, and he gave him an order, Mr. Paynter signed an order (produced). Toe body of the tourment 'was in witness's handwriting. Witness mentioned to Mr. Paynter that their terms were three months credit, and also gave him a verbal list of the customers. The goods were not bought on the sale or return principal, and no mention Was made of such being the case. He called at Mr, Paynters in March or Aprii, for payment, and Mr, Paynter said he had not done so well with the goods, and had offered to send on some money. Witness took one order in Runcorn, and went to Mr. Paynter and said he; could supply it if he cared to do so. The customer was the Executors of the late Mr. Speakman.—Uross- examined : He load called upon the defendants for some years, but never up to December got an order. Paynter asked for the wholesale prices,and upon getting them he gave the order produced. This, witness contradicted later, and he told Mr. Paynter that he would make him agent. He asked Paynter to buy some gold paint and stains and told him they would make him the wholesale agent for Widnes, Garston, Runcorn, and Frodsham for their "Queen of Shebah" gold paint as he didn't care about travelling in the district. Mr. Paynter did not then ask what terms he should have. Mr. Paynter did say he thou zht he could not find sale for the articles. He write memorandum saying that the goods ordered by Mr. Paynter were for Widnes, Garston, Runcorn and Frodsham. Witness asked him to permit him to send the goods ; but defendant did not say he would only accept them on sale or return. Defendant did not, in March, say to him that he could not dis- pose of the stuff, and it would be better to send it back to the firm. He went to Mr. Speakman's and got an order for some gold paint which he told him would come from the defendant. He did not ask anyone to purchase " Queen of Shebah " gold paint at Speakman's. He told Mr. Speakman that Mr. Paynter was the agent for the town, and is would come through him. He knew that Mr. Speakman had refused 'to pay Mr. Paynter, but did not know upon what grounds. He had called later upon Speakman and asked whether the order had been executed. Mr. Speakman offered to pay, but he refused to accept pay- ment—Mr Thomas Coppock, testified to being the plaintiff.—ln ansvrer to His Honour witness said that [ the goods had been purchased by Mr Paynter upon his own account,and that they did not in any way recognise him as an agent of theirs.—His Honour drew attention to the fact that Mr. Betts had written a document to Mr Paynter upon which he stated that the goods were for Widnes, Garston, Runcorn and Frodsham.—Witness thought the reason for the mention of the town wae that the traveller thinking that they were not good towns for him had made them over to the defendant.— The detence was that Mr. Paynter had accepted the goods upon sale or return on the understanding that he was agent for the plaintiff for the four towns named. The traveller Betts had been in the habit of calling upon him for many years but had never been given an order before the sth of December last. On that date owing to the inducement opened out to him be signed an order for the goods to be delivered as agent. —Evidence of considerable conversations was given,ard Mr. Robert Thomas Stringer testified to giving Mr. Betts an order for gold paint Sec. which was supplied by Mr. Paynter, He had declined to pay Mr. Paynter, however, because he ordered it for the defendant Corn- pany.—His Honour, in summing up, said the question was a broad issue for the jury to decide the term; of the contract between the parties, and impressed upon them the desirability of taking full cognisance of documentary evidence eepecial.y where witnesses statements were so considerably at variance.--After a lengthy deliberation ~.he jury returned a verdict for the defendant. Judgment was :'ntered accordingly.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
YOUNG WIFE DESERTED AT Sr. HELENS.

The St. Hi lens magistrates bad before them on Mon- day, a colliery contractor named Edward Holden, living at 6, Back Sutton-street, on a charge of wife desertion. Complainant said her husband earned about £3 a week. but he had regularly abused her since tele married him three years ago. She was then only sixteen, while he was ten years older. He was in the habit of assaulting her and making accusations u7aintit her which vrera not true. Complainant's grandrno her gave evidence and stid Holden was jealou4 of his own shadow. Defen- dant, who had put his wife and child out of the house, offered to take them back again, but the bench granted the woman a maint,nance order of 15s a week. THE STERILISED MILK EXPERIMENT AT ST HELENS.

At the meeting of the St. Helens Health Committee on Wednesday, Alderman J Forster, chairman, said that a report had been prepared of the Health Congress at Aberdeen. which was attended by a deputation from the Corporation. The experiment in infants' milk supply that was being carried on at St. Helens was a subject that was very much talked about. He should be very much surprised if a good many towns in the country did net follow their example. It was quite evident all the sanitary men were agreed that it was a very lam, step in the right direc- tion.—Alderman Sinclair : Is there a discussion reported on the matter ?—The Chairman said it was discussed in connection with a paper read by Dr. Hope, of Liverpool, on " Infant Mortality," in which he spoke in terms of very high praise of what had been and was being done in St. Helens. The medical officers of Manchester and Glasgow, and Dr. Vacher, of the Cheshire County Coun- cil, spoke of St. Helens having taken the right step. The committee would be interested in a report that he had before him of Dr. Harris's paper on the "Infants' Milk Sopply Depot," which was read by him at the Ipswich Congress.

div.head: PROMOTION OF RUNCORN POSTMASTER.
div.p: PROMOTION OF RUNCORN POSTMASTER.

It will be with mingled feelings that the Runcorn people will receive the announcement that Mr. W. K. Orrell, postmaster, Runcorn, has been promoted to take charge of the more extensive and important district of St. Austell in Cornwall. While congratulating Mr. Orrell upon his well merited promotion, the people of Runcorn will deeply regret his departure from their midst. 'Deo promotion, no doubt, is nighly acceptable to Mr. Orrell, but at the same time this recognition of his long and faithful service seems somewhat tardy. We believe Mr. Orrell early in 1892 received a much more valuable offer which for reasons best known to himself he refused and it is to be hoped that the present promotion is only the prelude to still further advancement. Although only just past the meridian of life, Mr. Orrell can beast of over forty years service. As a young boy he commenced his career as a telegraphist at Loetock Junction, Bolton, this native place, under the old Magnetic Company and after. words as instructor he had a very active career. He spent some time at Burnley and at Hunts Bank, Man- chester, and when only 15 years of age he was sent to Liverpool and appointed clerk in charge of St. George's Dock branch office. Then followed five years in charge of the Wigan office and three years at Bolton. In 1870 the Magnetic Company was transferred to the Post Office and a few months afterwards Mr Orrell was sent to the York-street bead telegraph office, Manchester. Here his abilities were r.till further recognised and he was transferred to the East London district and placed in charge of the principal branch Post Office. In 1889 he was app Anted postmaster of Runcorn and his eleven years in the Cheshiie pest have been years of progress in postal administration. When be took charge the Post Office was located in the dingy, inconvenient premises in [sigh-street, but since then the Post Office on Savages Bridge has peen built—a building commodious, up to date in its arrangements and central. It may truly be said that during the period of Mr Orrell's control, local post office facilities have been revolution- ised in the interests of the public. He has caused sub- offices to be established at placee most easy of access and convenient to the public. Pillar boxes have been multi- plied. and the collection and the delivery of letters generally improved. Weston and Weston Point have also felt the advantages of his enlightened rule, and the previously benighted people of Rock Savage have had cause to rejoice. Personally, Mr. Orrel to um a colloquialism, is ever approachable, highly courteous, and full of zeal in the discharge of his oner- ous duties and he leaves Runcorn with the heartiest wishes for his future success and happinnese. Runcorn's loss is St Austell's gain. A successor to Mr. Orrell has not yet, we understand, been appointed.

The Newton detachment of the 6th V.B. returned on Saturday to Newton-le-Willows after a fort- night's sojourn in camp on Salisbury Plain. The detachment which numbered 73 men looked bronzed and seemed to have fully enjoyed their camp life The drill in canap was more vigorous than in previ- ous years. Ceremonial drill was entirely dispensed with and the men had all practical instruction. The commissariat staff was well organised and food ex- cellently served in consequence.

On Sun lay morning, at 2.30, Lady Delamere,wife of Lord Delamere, and daughter of the Earl of Enniskillen, gave birth to a sln and heir at Vale Royal, near Northwich, the ii.is-d7e seat of his ordship. Revision of the Voters' Lists.

Mr. James T. Foard, barrister, will attend at the Town Hall on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday, September 10th. 11th and 12th, for the purpose of revising the lists of voters for the Borough. Mr. William Holbrook, on behalf of t'ae Conservatives, will make 268 claims and objections, and Mr. John Clayton. on behalf of the Liberals, 266, making a total of 534. Bonus on Wages in the Bedstead Trade.

The bedstead trade is in a very disorganised state through the abandonment of the alliance sys- tem by a number of influential manufacturers. The makers remaining nominally in combination have intimated their inability to continue to pay the 40 percent. bonus OM wages which wa4 the workman s share of the increased profits secured by the alli- ance. The wages board, on which the manufac- turers and employees sit, met on Monday in Bir- mingham. An offer was forthcoming from the em- ployers to pay a bonus of twenty-five per cent. to their operatives, it being urged that this wag as much as the exigencies of competition would war- rant. The workmen will consider the proposal. Local Trades Unionism.

There was very little businesQ of public interest at the monthly fleeting of the Trades and Labour Council which was held at the Waggon and Horses Inn, Buttermarket-street on Tuesdav evening. A letter was received from the Town Clerk, stating that the Trades Council's letter with regard to the application for a room for the mmtingg at the Town Hall would be laid before the next meeting of the TOWR Hall, Park and Baths Committee. A me- morial and circular were received from the Lanca- shire Fsderation of Trades and Libour Councils on the subject of cheap trains for workmen. The cir- cular pointed out that the railway companies were bound to provide cheap trains under reasonable conditions, and it was proposed if necessary to petition Parliament on the subpet. Signatures to the memorial were invited, and the Secretary (Mr W Bullock) as instructed to obtain 50 signature forms. A letter was received from the Chamber of Commerce, stating that they would agree to the formation of a Concilistion Board, provided they were allowed a free hand in the election of their five representatives. This was agreed to.

div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
CHARGE AGAINST A SERVANT.-A. PAINFUL CASE.

On Monday morning at the Warrington Police Court, before Mr. F. Monks and other magistrates, Gertrude Sellars, servan•,awascnarged with having stolen from a bedroom at, 262, Manchester-road, some time between Saturday, the 28th July and Friday, the 17th of August, a lady's diamond riere, two blouses and other articles oi the total value of £l7, the property of Emily Charlotte Bennett. Defendant, who appeared to feel her position very keenly, was accommodated with a seat in the dock. She pleaded guilt; .—The Chief Constable said this was one of tbe most painful cases he had ever had te deal with in the whole of his experieuce. This young girl, not 17 years of age, came from a highly respectable family and prior t this :here had not been a shadow of anything against her. She was so highly recommended some three or tour weeks ago that she was taken into the service of Mr. Jeseph Bennett, cattle dealer, of 262, Manchester-road, as nurse-housemaid. She remained in his service until Friday night. During the time she was at the house Mrs. Bennett missed a number of articles, the most important of which were her engagement ring, a gold ring set with diamonds, and a scarf pin belong- ing to Mr. Bennett. Other articles of weariug apparel. belonging to Mrs. Bennett were also missed. She did not in any way suspect the girl until Friday night, the girl's night out, when she came to receive her wages, and Mrs. Bennett noticed she was wearing a chiffon tie which belonged to her (Mrs. Bennett). She accused the girl of havieg taken it. The girl denied the allegation very indignantly, but subsequently handed the tie to Mrs. Bennett. She then left the house and did not return until eleven o'clock at night. In her absence Mr. Bennett being suspicious examined the girl's box in the presence or nis wife and the other Servants, and found a number of blouses, a silver buckled belt, and several other articles belonging to Mrs Bennett.. Wnen the girl returned to the house she was accused of having taken the articles, and she had the effrontery to go down on her knees and protest to Heaven that see had never touched anything belonging to her mistress. She afterwards fsund that her box had bees examin.d, and the Liexr, morning slipped away from the houso about half-past seven. She was not seen again until she was arrested. He should have said that on Friday night Mr. Bennett t(sld the girt that if she would tell him where the ring was she would hear nothing further about the matter. She solemnly pro• tested that she knew absolutely nothing whatever abaut it. The matter was placed in the hands of the police, and the girl was arrested in Manchester-road, on Battle day afternoon by Detective Meacock. She was brought to the Police Station, and questioned about the ring. but would give no information. He (the Chief Con- stable) had an interview with her on the Saturday night, cud she then chose to give him certain informa- tion, as a result of which he visit-ml Mr. Bennett's house with Chief-Inspector Phillips. He made a search of the nurserY,.and the ring was found in the chimney. The girl now admitted the whole of the thefts, but Mr. Bennettovished him to say that considering her previ- ous character, her youth and the mental trouble she had experienced since the occurrence, he did not desire to press the charges in an undue way. He left the matter entirely in the hands of the magistrates. The girl, esho had been baited out, had, the Chief Constable added, suffered most poignantly.—The Chairman said that as Mr. Bennett did not press the case the magistrates were able to deal with the defendant under the First Offenders' Act. They hoped this would be a lesson to her. She would be bound over to be of good behaviour for six months.
ALLEGED INGENIOUS THEFT BY A BOY.

At the Warrington Police Court, on Wednesday, before Messrs. Birchall and Geddes, a boy named Thomas Jenks was charged with stealing by means of a trick, from Mary E:izabeth Willcocks, whilst in the Market Place at noon the previous day,the sum of 4s, the money of Charloqe Finch.—The Chief Constable asked for a remand as in addition to the charge that morning there wu d no doubt be several others. The pollee also wished to make at least two more arrests in connection with the thefts. This sort of thing had been a perfect scourge in Warrington for a considerable time, and the police had been very busy investigating cases. The thefts, were committed in a very ingenious manner, and reflected credit at least on the intelligence of the perpetrators if not on their honesty. Referring to the particular case before the magistrates, the Chief Con- stable said that Willcocks was the daughter of Mrs. Charlotte Finch who had a stall in the Mark.n and re- sided at 11, Foundry-street. On Wednesday forenoon she was standing et the stall when the prisoner,who was a perfect Stranger to her, came up and said "Your mother says you have to send her 45." The girl said "Tell my mother I want her"and the boy went away.He returned sometime afterwards and said "Your mother says you must send that money or she will rattle your ear- hole." Noeloubt overawed by the threat the girl parted with 4s and the boy went away. The mother subse- quently'came to the stall and informed the girl that she uid not send for the money. The matter was put in the hands of the police and later in the day the prisoner's mother came to Mrs Finch and asked her to square the matter, offering to return the 4s. This put the police on the track of the prisoner and it had since transpired that there was an organised gang of at least three, who committed these offences. In order to effect the arrest of the other two and to work up several other cases he asked for a remand for three days. —Prisoner was re- manded until to-lay.

FRlDAY—Before the Mayor (In the chair), Councillors Pier- point NinltasuANldSTmkßyethucrostwaaVEDMessrs Hepherd and Hayward. —The adjourned case in which William Owen, 108, Wilderspool-road, was summoned for using acowshed which was not registered, on March 12th came up for hearing.— Inspector Norman stated that the case was adjourned on defendant promising to discontinue keep- ing cattle. He had not done Bo and had made little or no improvement in the building. The drainage of the shed was defective and it was highly contrary to the bye- laws.—Defendant stated that he did not keep the cows in tbe Mei; they were simply milked in it.—The Mayor: It is just as important that the place where you milk the cows should be kept as clean and well ventilated as the place where you keep them regularly. It is of the greatest possible Importance to the health of the town that the various milk Shops and dairies inside the borough should be kept as free from contamination as can be done.—A fine of 20s and costs (£1 8s in all) was Imposed. Crossley-street. was summoned for using a slaughter house near Crossley street without having first obtained a license from the Health Committee on the 3rd inst.—lnspector Norman stated that at 4 p m. on the date in question he visited the defendant's premises Everall had a butcher's shop in Crossley-street: and adjoining it were a dwelling house and yard with an open shed behind. The yard in which the stied was built was very imperfectly paved. In the shed he found fixed hanging irons and hooks for alaughte lag purposes and two freshly dressed sheep were hanging on the hooks—By Mr. Browne: Defendant usually slaughtered at the Seven Stars, Bridge-street.—Mr. Browne, who appeased for the defendant. stated that Mr. Evora!! was exceedingly sorry for what bad occurred. Un. fortunately on the date in question a heavy storm occurred and defendant's men in order to avoid going through the town dressed the sheep in the shed. Tnere was nothing wrong with the sheep and the yard was 60 feet by 40 feet in dimensions. He would undertake that the offence was not repeated.— A fine of ha ant costs was imposed. Bore IN TROUBLE.—EIeven boys, named James Tranter. William Baxter. John Lowe. George Casey, Charles Casey, George Stevens, Arthur Stevens, John Dagnall, William Dagnall, George Jaundrell, and James Bruce, residing in the neighbourhood of Warburton-street and Winwick-road, were summoned for destroying a quantity of oats, the property of James Robinson. Avenue Farm, doing damage to the amount ot 21.—Mr. Taylor (Messrs. Gseenall and Buckton) prosecuted and stated that Mr. Robinson laad a field of oats on the north side of the Cheshire Lines Railway, adjoining Warburton-street. For some time past considerable damage had been done to) property in that neighbourhood by boys living about there. In consequence of which officers in plain clothes had been on duty t 3 endeavour to detect the offenders. Complaints had also been made of boys throwing stones at trsins as they passed. On the night of the 9th inst. P.C. Clough saw the defendants in company with five others get over a sleeper fence at the top of War- burtou-st. and enter Mr. Robinson's field in which oats were growing. After running about in it for about five minutes they got on the railway lines. They were driven back by a platelayer named Woods and P.C. ()lough caught Tranter and Baxter and obtained the names of the other boys from them They had all since admitted that they were in the field. The damage which had been done on this farm alone amounted to £2O a year.—William Dsgnall, whom the other defendants stated was not in the field was discharged and the other boys were fined 5s each. R.S.P.C.A. PPAPCOUTIoN.—WiIIiam Caldwell, Frodsham, was summoned for ill-treating a horse on the 6th inst by working it whilst it was in an unfit state.—lnspeetor Browne, R.5.P.0.A., stated that he saw the defendant in charge of a bay gelding attached to a carriers' cart laden with parcels *c. 'the horse was eery lame on the near hind leg.— Defendant said that he bought the horse a month ago for £lO. He had now sold it for 17s 6d in order that it might be destroyed.—Defendant was fined in the costs (LN.) jOBSCENE LANGUAGE.—For making use of obscene language in Garabaldi-street to the annoyance of residents George Aspinall was fined 10s and costs (21 in all), _ .

WIFE DESERTION—UNHAPPY MARRIED LIFE.—John Col- ton. 14, Bluecoat-street. was summoned for deserting his wife limma Callon on the 11th inst.— kir. Steel appeared for the complainant and defendant was represented by Mr Browne.—Mr. Steel said the parties were married on March 6th, 1898, and had two children. They had lived a very, uncomfortable life together and oa several occasions defen- dant had turned his wife out of the house. Six months after they were married he was bound over for assaulting her On Saturday night, July 28th, as defendant had not come home complainant went into the street to look for him. When he came up he used filthy language towards her, and r.told her to go into the house. When they got into the house defend- ant threatened to take her life and she was so afraid that she ran) out. Defendant did not admit her until two o'clock next morning when P.C. Cooper came to the house. On the following day he came home drunk at ten o'clock and after threatening his wife he ran at her in order ta strike her. She managed to get away from him and left the house. On Monday he would not go to work at all and was drinking all day. In the after- noon he pawned his best boots to get more drink, He came homedrunk at nine o'clock and called his wife filthy names. She lost her temper and called him an Irish fenian and he then put her out of the house. She had been to the house three times and on each occasion the door was fastened. Defendant had taken the furniture away and she had no home or maintenance. Defendant was a bolter down in the nine inch mill at Dallarn and on one occasion he told the magistrates in that Court that he cowld earn 9s a day. He (Mr. Steel) asked the Bench to make an order for 15s week.—Mr. Browne did not dispute the desertion but said that both parties were very bad tempered and got to high words. Defendant alleged that his wile neglected the child- ren. He earned only 28s a week. The magistrates granted an order for 15s a week and allowed lOs 6cl advocates fees.— M-. Browne remarked that he had never heard of such a large order being made in that Court.—The Mayor: It doem't matter, It is a record then. We have made an order and decline to discuss the matter with you. MONBAY.—Before Mr. F. Monks; (in the chair), Councillor
Smethurst and Messrs. Birettail, Hayward an:.l Wright

A PRODUCTIVE HEAD.—Kargaret Kelly, 3, -Lower Bank-street, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Bank-street, at a quarter past eight on Saturday night.—P.O. Corbett proved the case.- -Defendant produced a I trge quantity of hair which she said the police had pulled out ef her head. -Corbett said the defendant showed him the hair on Saturday and said her brother-in-law had pulled it out.---11r. Birchen ; I believe you showed that to the magistrates last week.—Defendant This is a fresh lot.— The Chairman: Your head must be wonderfully produotive.— The Chief Consttble ooserved that it was very fruitful both inside and out, hair outside and lies In.—P.O. Pennington gave evidence, and a fine of ss. and costs was imposed. A BERIOUI3 OeFENCE.—WARRING TO BoYEL—Jarvis Taylor 2, Back Haydock-stre:t ; John Rate, 32, Haydocis• street ; John Kirkham, 13, ilaydock-street ; John Lawless, 40, Haydock-street ; John Laugford, 63, Haydock-street and Joseph Hoyles,36,Turner-street were summoned for throwing stones on the London and North-Western Railway on July 13th.—They all pleaded guilty.—Detective-Inspector Atkins Lime-street Station, Liverpool, who prosecuted on behalf of th company, said the caarge was a very serious one. The defendants wrre geen on the bridge of the new road which crossed thr lirie between Arcley and Bank Quay. An engine was passing under and they threw a quantity of stones, one of which, said to have heen thrown by Taylor, rebounded from the tender and struck the driver in the back. When Taylor was c tught he had a quantity of stones in his posse- - lion. The defs.ndants threw at three different trains, and in one case a stone came through the spectacle glass of the engine. He need not remind the Bench what the con- sequences might have been had the fireman or driver been looking out. Fortunately neither of them was struck. He had been asked to request the Bench to deal severely with the boys. This sort of thing had been going on for a considerable time. —Defendants were ordered to be birched and detained et the Police Siation until six o'clock in the evening.
TUEsray.—Betne Alderman Sutton (In the chair) and Mr,
Birchall.

A. MIN IVDDED OF His WATCH AND CHAlN.—Margaret Oakes, a well-known character, and lilijah Monks, a young man residing at 48, Alkin-street. were charged with an in- decent offence on Town Hill at 10.30 the previous night, and Oakes was also charged with stealing from the person of Monks a silver watch and chaia value 4)3. —From the evi- dence it appeared that prisoners went on Town Hill for an im- proper purpose and were taken into custody by P.C.'s Turner and Whittaker. AI the Police Station Monks missed his watch and chain, and it was found in the woman's pocket. She said she did not know it was there.--The Chief Constable said that Oakes made her 24th appearance having been before the Court nine times within twe.ve months. Monks ap- peared to be a respectabo3 young mau.—Tbe Bench com- mitted Oakes to gaol for a month on the first charge and two months on the second, and fined Monks os. and costs with the alternative of seven days Imprisonment.

MONDAY. Before Messrs, A. Thorns and H. Reynolds.

AFTER 38 YEARS —fto,e Scott. an old woman, ;vas sum- moned by her husband. Benjamin Scott, for assaulting him on the 11th August.—Ar. Knowles appeared for the woman and pleaded not guilty. The complainant said he was a rag dealer and lived in Heath-road. He alleged that when he was giving the donkey his supper, his wife insulted him awfully He left er and she followed him to Mill Brow. He turned round to tell her to go home, when she struck him on the left side of the bead with an enamelled tin jug, making bloo,l fl4w like rain Bvery time he weut near the place she wa very violent with him. On this occasion she struck him about four times.—Mr. Knowles. tor the defence, said it was a pity this elderly couple " fell out" in this way. On the 4th August the husband oame to the little place of business and took away a quantity of iron which she had been collect- ing. He sold the iron for £5 10s. and from the 4th to the 11th he was spreeing with the proceeds, and he never gave her a penny. On the 24th he came to the place and brought a 3d loaf, and three eggs, which was en y important as showing the trifle he thought necessary for household requisites. She tried to get some money from him ; he offered her £2. but she refused RS she had to pay the persons who sold to her. She followed him into the Naviga- tion Inn and admitted that,she had struck him on the head with the jug because of the way he treated her.—The woman corroborated this statement and said she had been married to the complainant 36 years. The place had her husband's name over the door but it was bpught with her money.—The Bench dismissed the case.

COLLECTING A DEBT —Ellen Rose, a young married woman was charged with assaulting Emily Finney, shop- keeper, Waterloo-road. The detendkat pleaded guilty.—The complainant said that on the 4th August she went to the de- fendant's house and asked her if she could pay her any of the money she owed her. She replied she would send It down later. Witness replied that there was a man waiting for some money. With an oath defendant replied he could wait and struck witness on the breast knocking her to the ground. She bled very much from a wound on the head. She had been under the doctor's care since.—Caroline Robinson, a neighbour, corroborated, aud the defendant who was very aggressive in her behaviour was fined 20s and cosai 1.9 or in default 21 days imprison- ment.—The defendant: 1 shan't pay—not a halipenny.—The prisoner was then taken below to the cells. OBSCENE LANGUAGE.-1311z%beth Smith:km, an elderly woman, pleaded guilty to using obscene language in Cholmondeley Place. and on the evidence of P.C. Gilpin, she was fined 5s and costs. 8s 6d. MAINTENANCE.—WiIIiam Renny, was summoned for arrears of a maintenance order by his wife Lucy. The prisoner had been ordered by tee justices of Dale-street Police Court Liverpool, to contribute 10s per week and he was in arrears £8 8s Od.—The prisoner had £1 2s Od in his possession, and he agreed to give his wile £1 and keep up his payments. The warrant was thereupon witha. awn.
