div.p: rHE EXAMINER FRI DAY AUGUST 24, 1900.
(Copyright.)
ivauonna. Instead or an expression or stern reouxe, there seemed to be a look of sympathy and kind.. uess on her face.

Did the Holy Virgin love Joseph, her husband, even as other holy women loved the man of their choice, as Protestants had taught ? The thought was sacrilege, but was it true ? slt was very beautiful to him! He looked again, to see some expression of anger, but at that moment the sun broke out from behind the clouds, and as a sunbeam played on the Virgin's face the young monk thought he saw her smile. His dream was over.

Weeks passed away, and Brother Francis continued to discharge his duties at the monastery; but life was altogether changed. The memory of that after- noon became a Wonderful influence. He constantly called to mind the maiden he had seen in his dream. Even when he knelt at prayers he saw the sunny meadows and heard the singing of the birth. Presently he began to think seriously about the monastic life into which he had entered. He had been led to regard it as the highest form of exist- ence. What could be nobler than to spend one's years in prayer and devotion to holy things? This naturally led him to ask himself what was holy, and what was sinful. Was love sinful? Was it sinful to follow the promptings of the human heart? Was it holy to quench the most beautiful of desires? He could never live the full, rich, free life which other young men were living. After all, the holiness of a monastery was not positive, it was negative. A monk was largely a machine, and if his life were free from outward sin it was because it was free from outward temptation. Surely that was not the highest kind of virtue?

Ind he longed for love. Although he was scarcely conscious of it. he longed to behold in the flesh her of whom he had dreamt. Should he ever see her ? Should he ever hear her speak ? And, as if in answer to his question, the words of the song he had played mi ca e nto his mind:
"She is waiting somewhere, she I shall honour, She that I long for, my queen, my queen!"
One day the rector Of the monastery called Brother Francis to him.
"My son," said the rector, "I have work for you to do in London."

"Yes, father." "It will be necessary for you to cast aside the garb of your order, and dress as an ordinary English gentleman." "You mean the ordinary clerical attire 2" "No, my son. You must dress as a layman. It will be necessary, if you are to carry out the work you have to do." Brother Francis's heart seemed to grow too great for his bosom.
"A dispensation will be granted, so that you can move freely among people of the world, and act as one of them."

"Yes, father." The rector then told the young man of the work he was expected to do in London, and Brother Francis undertook it without question. In the order to which he belonged implicit obedience was one of the great virtues, and for many years he had been constantly taking lessons therein. Hi 3 experiences in London were a revelation to the young monk,- and for thearst time in his life he felt really happy. His liberty made existence alto- gether new, to be free from, monastic rule made him feel as a bird feels when it has escaped from its cage. He dreaded the day when his work should be accomplished, dreaded the thought of going back to the dreary routine of monastic life. And why should he go? Why could he not stay in the world and live the full, free life of the world which God has given to the sons of men? _ _ _

One day he went int,o- the country. He had been in London a week before an opportunity to do this had occurred. During his week of busy life, the face of his queen had seemed less real. While he had been in the monastery he had felt sure that she existed in actual life, but when he moved amidst the thronging millions of London doubts came into his mind. It seemed foolish to believe that the fancies which had possessed him while he played the organ in the monastery church had any exist- ence in actual life. Once out in the country, how- ever, and the vision became real again. He had had no object in going into the country save to wander among the fields, and to call to mind the scene which had passed before his eyes as he sat in the church; but he hoped at times that he should see his queen in the flesh. But, dreamer as he was, he laughed at the thought. Nevertheless, the laugh was full of sadness. He got out of the train at a little roadside station, and, seeing a footpath through the fields, he left the main road, and followed it. Brother Francis tried to think he had seen it all before, but he knew it was not so. The countryside was fair to behold, but it did not correspond with the dewy meadows and the rippling river he had seen as he had played the love-song. • After following the course of the footpath for some distance, he came upon a country lane. On each side the grass grew, and it looked as though scarcely a conveyance passed from morning to night." Everything was quiet, too—not a house, not a human being was in sight. There was no sound- ing water near, but the birds sang blithely. The air was delicious, and the sun poured its generous warmth upon him. A pleasant languor crept over him, and, seeing a spreading tree in a meadow near, he went towards it, and lay down beneath its shady branches. How long he remained there he scarcely knew. Whether he had been asleep or not he could not tell, but presently he was aroused by the sound of angry voices. Starting up, he rushed into the lane, and saw a boy of twelve struggling in the grasp of a tramp. The lad fought bravely, but the tramp was a large-limbed, power- ful fellow. _ _

Brother Francis knew bet little of the ways of the .world, but he instantly surmised the meaning of what he saw. Evidently this well-dressed lad was out walking alone, and the tramp, seeing him, and knowing that no one was likely to hinder him, determined to possess himself of anything the boy might possess. "Give me back my watch!" he heard the boy cry angrily; "it is not yours. Give it to me!" The tramp laughed. "No, youngster, I ain't a-goin' ter do nothin' the sawt ; but, just ter be quits, I'll tike thet 'ere scawf pin and those foo loose coins wot's a-rettlin' in yer pocket," and he held the lad firmly in his powerful grasp. "No, you shan't," said the boy, "you shan't," and he struggled and fought with all the determination that characterises the best specimens of our English lads.

"Stop it naa," said the tramp; "if yer doaWt I'll spile thet 'ere jib er yore's. I wornts ter do this thing in a gentlemanly wy. but if yer won't be reasonable—well, you must tike the consequences." But the boy continued to fight and struggle, in spite of the fact that the tramp held him with a grip of iron: Years of monastic life had done a great deal to deaden the power of definite action in the young monk's life, and for time he seemed incapable of rendering any hell, I,riy. who was at the mercy of the evil fello,. ' -ld him. But no system of training can altcgetinit —stroy a man's manhood. It may render him awkward, undecided, and for a time incapable, but there comes a moment when the power of a negative life is broken. Thus it came about that while Brother Francis stood for some little time speechless and inert, no sooner did he see the tramp lift his right hand to stril the boy than he bounded over the hedge like a "Let go that lad!" he cried. 1 This unexpected interference caused the tz-,.,inp to drop his hold. He looked at the young man attentively, and then walked away. "All right, guv'nor." he said with a grin. "He's got my watch," shouted the boy. "Give the boy his watch," cried Brother Francis. "Shawn't," was the tramp's reply. "Please make him," said the boy; 'my sister gave it to me only yesterday for a birthday present. Please make him return it."
I

Brother Francis stood before the tramp. "Give the boy his watch," he repeated. "1 in't er got his wotch, " was the reply; "this 'ere wotch wos gived to me only yisterday, by my honly sister, and this 'ere young cove wanted ter tike it from me."
"Give it back, or I shall make you," said Brother Francis.

The tramp looked at him attentively. The young monk was by no means muscular; long years of monastic life do not tend to make a man an athlete. "Well, guv'nor, I shall be werry pleased if yer'll try it on," grinned the fellow, placing himself in a boxing attitude. Reeking nothing of consequences, Brother Francis made a leap at the fellow, for which he received a stunning blow between the eyes; but he succeeded in getting hold of the collar of the tramp's coat, and to this he held fast.

"I shall not let you go until you return the lad's watch," he panted. . How long the struggle continued he knew not. He was totally ignorant of the art of self-defence, and he was far weaker than the stalwart thief, but he held him fast, nevertheless. Again and again did the other try to throw him off, but in vain. The dogged persistency of the Englishman revealed itself in spite of the influence of monasticism. He felt his head swimming, and sparks of light flashed before his eyes, but he never relaxed hie hold. His breath came thick and fast, but he nevei dreamt of giving up. At length, however, he knew that his strengtl was giving way. The fellow gave a terrible blow, and one of his hands was useless; then he began tc fear that his help would be of no avail. But iE spite of the tramp's efforts he still held him fast. "Give the boy his watch," he said hoarsely, and after that remembered nothing save the sounds of a strange voice, for a delicious kind of laneuor crept
over nun, anu wen everytning ocean-4e as !lowing to him.

When he awoke to consciousness he was lying ov the greensward by the roadside, and by his sidi knelt a man of, perhaps, fifty years of age. "That's right, you are better now," he heard a voice say heartily. "Is the fellow gone?" asked Brother Francis. "Yes, he's gone, worse luck!" "Has the boy got his watch?" "Oh yes; he's got it." "That's all right," said the young monk dreamily. "Lift your left arm," said the man. He tried, but failed to do so. "I am afraid it's broken," said the man. "I'm glad the boy has got his watch," said Brother Francis.
"Yes, thanks to you, he has. It's my boy you helped, sir, my only son." The monk but dimly understood What the other meant.

After that he became unconscious again. He had a vague idea that he was taken somewhere, where he knew not, neither did he care; he also thought that the tramp followed him, and constantly pulled his arm, which caused him great pain. When he became conscious again he found himself lying on a bed, in a well-furnished room. "You'll be all right now," said a voice which he had not heard before. "You had a nasty blow on the head, and your shoulder was out of joint, but no bones are broken. In a day or so you will be as well as ever."
"Are you a doctor ? " he asked dreamily. "Yes." "Where am I ?"

"You are at my house," said the man who had spoken to him by the roadside, "and you must stay here a few days now." "And your son?" "Oh, he's all right—thanks to you. But we'll not talk of that now. How do you feel yourself, sir?" . _

"I feel dazed, that's all. - I have iio pain." "That's right, take it quietly," said the doctor. "I shall want you to sleep a few hours, and to- morrow you'll feel much better." When he awoke it was early morning. He heard the song of birds as they sang among the branches of the trees outside the house.
He sat up in bed. His shoulder was painful, other- wise, save for a sense of weariness, he felt no illness.
"Where am I ? " he thought. "Whose house is this? Well, I shall know presently, I suppose. Hark, what's that ? "

The blood mounted to his face, his heart beat wildly. "It's her voice ! " he cried—"aye, and it's the same song!" He listened eagerly, and the refrain of a song, sung by a sweet girlish voice, was wafted to his ears. "I've been roaming, I've been roaming, Midst the grass and flowers so sweet, And I'm coming, yes, I'm coming, With the dewdrops on my feet."

"I shall see her, I shall see her, my queen, my queen ! " he cried. The fact that he was a priest was unreal to him. It was not until the next day that he was allowed to come downstairs; but his host, and the boy he had helped, visited him in his bed- room.

He gave his name as Francis Lister. Somehow he shrank from telling them that he was a monk; besides, he was longing for the time to come when he should see the one who had been singing outside his bedroom window. He asked no questions con- cerning her. He concluded that she was the sister who had given the boy, whose name he had dis- covered to be Robert Thornton, the watch he had been so anxious to retain.
Only once did he hear news concerning her, and that was from Robert's father.
"My daughter is very anxious to see you, and to thank you for your kindness and bravery," said Mr. Thornton.

"Bravery said the young monk, as if in wonder. "What do you mean?" He was thinking all the time of his queen, he who was a priest. As yet, however, he had not realised that the passion that filled his heart would be regarded by his Superior as a temptation from the devil. Nay, though he had dreamt so much about love, he did not know what it meant.

When he saw her, she was altogether different from his dream. This was no blue-eyed, golden- haired, fair-skinned maiden. Her hair was as black as the raven's wing, her eyes were like sloes, her skin was clear but dark, her cheeks glowed with tha hue of health. His dream was not fulfilled, then. The face of the maiden in his day-dream was not the face of Laura Thornton.

Brother Francis stayed at Mr. Thornton's house three days, at the end of which time be said he must return to London. He had not revealed the fact that he was a monk; he dared not. And yet his dream had not come to pass. He talked for hours with Laura Thornton; he admired her beauty; but even his father confessor would not have condemned the thoughts he entertained towards her. She was the only woman he had ever conversed with, and naturally she influenced him greatly, but she was not the one of whom he had dreamt. He tried to analyse his feelings. He called to mind the thoughts which passed through his mind as he sat at the organ that day. "It was only a dream," he said. "It never formed a part of my life. Well, lam glad that my illusion is gone. I shall be able to go back to my work now. But suppose she had been like-" A look of fear came into his eyes. "I am afraid I had forgotten my vows," he said. This was the evening of the day before he returned to London.

Up to the present he had taken no long walks. His encounter with the tramp had affected him more than the doctor had thought. He did not know of the weakening effect of long vigils, and prayers, and fasting. This evening, however, he was walk- ing through the meadows which surrounded the house; by his side was Laura Thornton. They had gone some little distance and were returning home- ward.
"You go back to-morrow morning, Mr. Lister ?" said the girl. "Yes." "How strangely we have been thrown together," she said.
" Yes, very strangely." "I wonder if we shall ever meet again after to- morrow ? " _

"Meet again? Why, yes!" he said, and then he remembered his calling. "Do you care?" he con- tinued. "Do you care?" "I do, indeed," she replied. "You have been very kind to us. You have rendered us a great service." "Is that all ?"

He did not know what he was saying. He was blindly following the leadings of his heart, recking not of the consequences. "No, it is not all," she answered. "None of us will soon forget your visit. Somehow, you aro different horn the rest of our friends."

What made Laura Thornton speak like this she could not have told. Nevertheless, she knew she spoke the truth. The quiet reserve which character- ised the young monk, the strange yearning look in his eyes, affected her in spite of herself. She looked up into his face, and he looked into the depths of her eyes. What he saw he could not tell, but he knew that his heart seemed torn from J-i4s:rn, and his life shaken to the very foundom Tevertheless, he spoke no word during tneir 1 ; ard journey.

When Brother Francis returned to the monastery he made confession to his Superior. He told his story from beginning to end. The old man listened gravely. "It is a grievous sin," he said; "remember your vows." "I do," replied Brother Francis, "but ever since I looked into her eyes there has been a fire in my heart." "And you have struggled?" "I have not slept an hour since I last spoke to her" he said. "I have fought and prayed—in vain." "If you continue to love her, you will be damned for ever," said the rector. Days, weeks, months passed away, and Brother Francis became worn to a shadow. He had fasted, prayed, suffered penance, but the fires of love still burnt within him. The face he had seen in his dream had faded away, but the real face of the raven-haired, dark-eyed girl with whom he had spoken was with him day and night. The flash of those great eyes into which he had looked had burntinto his very soul. His brother monks were commanded to pray for him, and he was commanded to torture his body by means of flagellation and scourging. Still in vain. "Do you ever entertain hopes of seeing this woman again ?" asked his confessor, after he had for the hundredth time told his story. "No," replied the monk. "And you have heard no word, had no message from her since you left the house of her father?" "No," replied Brother Francis. Again the rector applied the remedies of the Church, but again in vain. "I tell you," he said at length, "unless you destroy this unholy love, and drive this woman from your mind, you will be damned for ever." Brother Francis thought over these words raspy times, then he fell to reading the words of his Master, and the Apostles who followed Him. Presently he came to the Epistle of John. "For love is of God," he read, and 'God is love." He asked his confessor what this meant, but he received no reply; instead the older priest repeated his former threat: "Unless you drive this woman from your mind, you will be damned for ever!! Again the monk thought, read the Scriptures, and prayed. "If love will damn me for ever, then I must be damned for ever," he said at length. And as he spoke a new light shone in his eves.

The annual inspection bill in connection with the Ist V.B South Lancashire Regiment was held at the Drill hall on Monday evening, when about a hun- dred couples were present. The band of the battalion under the conductorship of Mr. J T Richardson, bandmaster, played for dancing, which commenced at half-past eight and was kept up until two o'clock the following morning. Colour-sergeant Spencer officiated as M. C. The refreshment department was under the management of Colour-Sergeant Cliffe, end Sergeant Connor had charge of the cloak room. The Charles Middleton Scholarships. Particulars are published in our advertising columns with reference to the Charles Middleton Scholarships for boys. There will be one senior scholarship value £9 first year, £l2 second year, and £l5 third year. It is stipulated that candidates must be under 17 and educated at elementary schools in Warrington, and the scholarships will be awarded on the result of past examinations of the Science and Art Department. There will also be two junior scholarships, value £4 first year, £5 second year, and £6 third year, to be awarded on the result of a special examination held September 11th. In this case candidates must be pupils of elementary schools in Warrington. With regard to entrance scholarship for girls (donation of Mr F W Monks), there will be one icholarship, value .£.5 for one year. div.head: MONK'S LOVE STORY.
div.p: A MONK'S LOVE STORY.
BY . JOSEPH HOCKING, Author of "All Men Are Liars," "The Story of Andrew Fairfax," "The Birthright." Etc., &c.

Brother Francis sat in the monastery church. He had gone thither to pray, and after spending some time in meditation on religious things he went to the organ, and began to play. He loved music, and it often gave him pleasure and comfort amidst the dreary routine of his daily life. For it was dreary. Brother Francis was only a young man of three-and- twenty, and his clean-shaven face gave him the appearance of a boy. He had bee-a led to accept the priesthood of the Roman Catholic Church as a vocation when quite a lad. Both his parents had died when he was vet:. young, and his guardian was easily persuaded by- the priest, who visited his house, that the child had a vocation for the priesthood. When spoken to con- cerning his future, and fascinated by the picture the priest drew of the religious life, the imaginative boy consented willingly to become a novice, and go through the necessary training in order to become a holy priest of God. Of course he scarcely knew what such .a step meant. The vows, which he eventually would have to take, seemed by no means terrible. Poverty, chastity, and obedience seemed to the boy beautiful ideals, and the thought of becoming a priest was full of charm. What boy realises the meaning of poverty? Besides, in the priesthood, his wants would be cared for. As for what was implied by the word chastity, the lad's mind was a blank. Celibacy was only a name, and no whisper came into his heart concerning the longings which might one day be aroused. Obedience might be hard, but he was of a religious turn of mind, and was sure that he would never wish to disobey his superior. When the time for taking his final vows came he had no misgiving, no doubt. He knew nothing of the world, for all information concerning outside life was kept from him. As for women, he had not spoken to one for many years. His nature had been bent and moulded according to the ideas of his order; and although he could not help a feeling of sadness creeping into his heart as he finally cut himself from the world, no positive doubt entered his mind and heart. He still remained in the monastery, for his abilities fitted him to become a teacher in certain branches of knowledge. The name he bore as a boy was almost forgotten. He was called Brother Francis, after the saint he had chosen, and, while he was not happy, the negative peace of his life had not been disturbed. I have given this brief sketch of Brother Francis's life because it seems necessary, if the reader will really sympathise with the story I have to tell. It had been a dark, dreary day, and the clouds had hung heavily in the sky for many hours, even though it was April, that month when the primroses peep forth and the lilacs prepare to display their beauty. And, as I said. Brother Francis had gone into the monastery church to pray, and had after- wards found his way to the organ. At first he played some of the music so popular in the Romanist Church, but afterwards he took to dreaming, and the organ was the medium through which he told his dreams. As he played there came to his mind a song which he had heard one of the priests sing on one of the feast days when the discipline of the monastery had been relaxed. He had thought nothing of it at the time, because songs of various orders were sung, and were regarded as forming a part of the innocent amusement of the Brothers on festive occasions. Now, however, it had a new meaning, and as he played the music on the organ he forgot his surroundings, forgot that he was in a building consecrated to holy deeds and holy thoughts. He remembered the words, remem- bered them plainly, especially the first verse, and in his heart he sang them, even while he played the melody.

"When and how shall I earliest meet her? What are the words she first will say? 'By what name shall I learn to greet her? I know not now, it will come some day. With the self-same sunlight shining upon her, Shining down on her ringlets' sheen! She is waiting somewhere, she I shall honour, She that I long for, my queen, my queen!"

The memory of the song aroused longings in Brother Francis's heart to which he had hitherto been a stranger. He forgot his vows, forgot all the weary years he had spent in seclusion. It was as though he had been asleep, and his heart awakened to a new life. The sentiment of the song filled him, the thought in the mind of the man who wrote it possessed him. He found himself longing for love, longing for the presence of a pure maid who should be the queen of his life. The objects by which he was surrounded had faded away. The pictures of saints and martyrs which hung on the wall were as nothing. He was there alone in the church, with his thoughts, his longings, and the organ. He was no longer a monk, but a man; no longer a negative thing whose heart's longings were stultified, but a lover whose blood surged madly through his veins, and whose heart was filled with a great, o4er-mastering desire. For the moment, at all events, the natural promptings of the human heart had destroyed the effects of penances and vows.

He played on dreamily, thinking only of the first verse of the song. He was away from the gloomy monastery; away from the sound of monks mumbling prayers in Latin; away from the sophistries whereby he had tried to teach the reasonableness of Roman dogmas; away from all man's conceptions of religion; away in the country, where music floated everywhere, and where the air was laden with the perfume of May flowers. He fancied himself wandering through meadows where daisies and buttercups grew, he saw the white hawthorn blossoms on the hedgerows, he heard the birds singing, and their songs mingled sweetly with the rippling of running waters. "She is waiting somewhere, she I shall honour, She that I long for, my queen, my queen!"

These were the words that filled his mind, and he played the music which had been set to them. Was he asleep? Had you asked him afterwards he could not have told you. His eyes were open, but he did not see the walls of the church.
"She is waiting somewhere, she I shall honour," was his thought, and so in his dream he wandered along the meadows on a beauteous May morning, while the sun drank up the dew.
Presently his heart gave a bound. Someone was coming. Was it she ?

In his fancy he saw a sweet maid coming towards him. Be saw her plainly. She was all that his heart desired, and he felt that he loved her with all the strength of his being. She was his queen. She was dressed all in white, even as a maid should be dressed on a May morning. In one hand she carried a hat, and this she swung to and fro as she walked. He was glad that it did not cover her golden locks, or shade the brightness of her shining blue eyes. He saw the healthful flush on her cheeks, and the parting of the rosy laughing lips. Oh, if he could kiss them, he who had never kissed a maid in his life!

She came towards him, tripping lightly over the dewy grass. Hark, she was singing! "And I'm Coming, yes, I'm coming, With the dewdrops on my feet I " He held his breath. This was his queen, here was the goal of his.heart's desire! He played on, hot knowing what he was doing. Somehow the organ had become a necessary part of his dream; it translated the visions and the longings of his heart into reality. The maiden came nearer to him, he saw her plainly. Her every feature was clear to him, he could see the flash of her eyes and the shape of her face. So close was she that it seemed as though by stretching out his hand he could take her silken hair in his hand and fondle it. Her parted lips revealed the pearly whiteness of her teeth; nay, he almost felt her warm breath on his cheeks. His heart burnt within his bosom like a mighty fire. His queen had come to him! He spoke no word, but in his heart he sung the last lines of the song he had been playing all the time:

"And I'll give my heart to my lady's keeping, And ever her strength on mine shall lean; And the stars they may fall and the saints may be weeping Ere I cease to love her, my queen) my queen!" He opened his mouth to speak, her face was close to his own, her hand was outstretched, he saw the lovelight in her eyes, and there seemed no shadow in the sky of his life, when- The clang of the monastery bell! He awoke!

Had he been asleep? Where were the dewy meadows, the scent of spring flowers? Where the queen of his life? looked around, and saw nothing but the old gloomy church, on the walls of which hung, to him, hideous daubs supposed to represent martyred saints. Then his eves turned towards the figure el the

The sixth annual show in connection with the Hatton Amateur Horticultural Society was held at Hatton Cottage, by permission of Mr R I Wynne Jones on Thursday last. The weather was all that could be desired and there were large numbers of visitors to the show, 'buses being run from Warrington. Th number of entries was satisfactory and the exhibits were of good quality. A splendid colt ,ction o iso: house plants, lbnt by Sir Gilbert Greenall Bart, was on view, and was much admired. An interesting exhibit was a hive of bees, which was shown by Mr Willi4m Cartwright, of Moore. div.head: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.

A KIDNAPPING CASE—A cradle. A REGIMENT OF THE "LINE" The railway "guards." THERE is a good deal of difference between the "book of the day" and a day-book. Luck is a happy combination of accidents; but it requires brains to combine accidents. EVERY man has two wives; the one he has and the one he thinks he has. ANOTHER MATT.—Jack: "Is Charlie a man to be trusted ?" Fred : "I'd trust him with my life." Jack: "Oh, yes, I know. But would you trust him with a sovereign ?" SHE: "I hate my name—it's SO hard to write in the sand." Ho: "Do you think you could write mine more easily?

FRIEND (to Satupon) : "I don't see what your wife has got to grumble at." Satupon : " Unfor- tunately, she's got me !" KEAN : "Isn't your wife afraid to drive that horse ?" Steam: "Not at all. It's the people she meets who are scared." MRS. PASSY—" Everybody says my daughter got her beauty from me. What do you say to that?" Mr. Witts—" Well, I think it was very unkinl of her to take it from you." THE PROFESSOR SOLILOQUISES. "Yes, my memory is ccrtatuly getting better. Now I re- member distinctly enough that my wife told me to tie a string about this finger. If I only could think what for !"
"Hi ! you're dropped your paint all over me !" Painter (cooly) : " Well, you want a new coat of some sort !"

A SCIENTIFIC paper tells us that a bee can move more than twenty times its own weight. This is greatly under-estimating the power of the bee. We have known it to propel a lourteen-stone man several feet into the air.

A SPEEDY RECOYERY.—Jimmy : "Are you back to school already? I thought you were good for three or four day's." Tommy "Well, me mother wouldn't let me go out, even after three o'clock. Might as well be in a hospital." A GOOD OFFEIt.—" I will save you a thousand nds," said an Irishman to an old gentleman, "if don't stand in your own light." " How ?" u have a daughter, and you intend to give her thousand as a marriage portion." "I do." Sir, I will take her with nine thousand." IN THE LAND 0' CAKES.—First Tourist: "How are you going to spend to-morrow ?" Second Tourist : " Well, if the weather is at all good, I'm going to Scone." First Tourist : "Bat what if the weather is bad?" Second Tourist : "Then I'm going to loaf." Too Mccu.--" And," were the concluding words of the professor's le,-Aure to the medical students, "do not promise too much. I know a physician of real ability who promised a patient, whose legs he had just amputated, that he would have him on his feet within two weeks."

SO UNNECESSARY. —He : "The fortune-teller described you exactly, and said that I would marry you." She " Don't you think it was a waste of money to conhlt her ? " He " Why ?" She : "I could have told you the same thing myself. DOHERTY : Do you think your father would offer personal violence if I were to ask him for you ?" Mabel: " No ; but I think he will if you don't."
HIS YEARNING. - Mrs. Flint (sceptically): " H'm ! What kind of a job do you want?" Seldom Fedd (with surprising candour) : "Any kind of a job dat I can't git, mum."

HIS VIEW OF THE MATTER. —" At any rate," said the cheerful•minded man, "though this is a cold and disagreeable day, it brings us at least one day nearer summer." " Yes," growled his friend, the pessimist, "and it brings us one day nearer next winter."

SOME OTHER BOY.—lndignant Citizen: " Say ! Your boy threw a atone at me just now and barely missed me." Mr. Grogan: " Yez say he missed ye?" "That's what I understood myself to re- mark." "It was not my bye." AN Indian chief beliig iked his opinion of a cask of Madeira wine which had been presented to him, said he thought it was juice extracted from woman's tongue and lion's heart, for after he had drunk of it he could talk for ever, and fight any- body. AWKWARD Horseman: "Stupid boy, what do you keep running beside me for ?" "Please, sir, 4;you'll be tumbling down in a bit, then I shall get aixpiance for ketching your 'oss." PUTTING HIS FOOT IN Ir.—She: "Don't you think Mrs. Wapsley is a beautiful woman?" He: "She is a beautiful woman—the most beautiful woman, I think, I have ever seen." She (after he has gone): "I wonder if he has always been such a fool, or whether it has just begun to grow on him lately." .

A WISE LAD.—A nhoohnaster was one day in- structing his class when, wishing to simplity a cer- tain point by an every-day illustration, he asked, "Have any of you boys ever stirred up a wasp's nest?" "Yes, sir ; -I have," said one of the smaller boys. " Well, what was the result?" "Please, kir, I Oilret wait to see," said the boy. OTHER FAT:Hi:AS AHED LIKnviSE.----" Hers; you've been telling me all along," said the bright- faced young wife, "what a wonderful cook your mother was. And now Aunt Jane has just told m 2 that your father was a chronic clzautie." Well, you see," the young husbaal muneured, with sizh, " melher 'win by practising - - • -r. athety, A ItAr4 liiiTtVA-3:2.--A well-known crofter coutew.d to the following rather amusing exper- ience:- Having secured a hare in a snare set by him he was unexpectedly come upon by a gamekeeper, but none abashed and with an aggrieved air he cried to the keeper while throwing away the hare, "1 dinna mind ye shooting o'er my peeps or tramp- ing o'er my drills, but I'll be hanged if I 'Met you tether your hares amongst them." A LARY in a registry office observed, "I am afraid that that little girl won't do for a nurse; she is too small ; I should hesitate to trust her with the baby ; she would be sure to drop it out of her arms." "Her size, madam," said the clerk, "we look upon as her greatest recommenda- tion. "Indeed, but she is so very small." "I know she is diminutive; but you should remember that when she drops a baby it doesn't have very far to fall."

" PRAPS you'll tell me what you think would be a fair charge?" said the seaside landlady, as she parted from the Brownlow family after a fierce dispute about the "extras" in the bill. "Yes, madam," said Mr. Brownlow, "I will ! I think a fair charge would be extorting money by false pretences and violence' and a fair sentence penal servitude for life. Good morning to you, madam !"

REASSITRING.—Mexicans are not very fond of Spaniards, and jokes are constantly cropping up in Mexico illustrative of the arrogance of the Spanish character. One now current in Mexico runs as follows: A Spaniard arrived at Vera Cruz and stepped ashore just as an earthquake occurred. Putting on a benign smile, he said, "Tremble not, Earth; I am not going to harm thee."

WEIGHT WILL TELL,—While a judge was giving his charge to the jury in a burglary ease, one of the jurymen fainted. His lordship had just said impressively : " Gentlemen of the jury, in arriving at a verdict, you must take the testimony of the witnesses for the defence into consideration and give them full weight." At the word, "And give them full weight," the juryman swooned away. He was a coal-dealer

SERJEANT BALLANTYNE had always a good story to tell. "I remember," relates a writer, "that during the Tichborue trial a counsel who had made his name notorious was swaggering about the num- ber of distinguished persons who had attended one of his receptions. I give you my word, sir,' said he, that on the occasion in question there was a line of carriages from one end of our street to the other.' '0 course there was,' replied Ballantyne you live opposite a cab-stand!' A friend of mine who was rather fond ot boasting of his con- nection with the British Army, on the strength of being an officer in the Militia, was one evening dis- cussing the Indian Mutiny. Observing that the Serjeant was smiling a trifle contemptuously, he turned on him. I dare say you think I know nothing about it,' he said rather angrily; tell you I was in Calcutta all through 1857—and yet you imagine I had nothing to do with the Indian Mutiny ? " Nothing to do with the Indian Mutiny?' repeated Ballantyne, with a drawl. Why, my dear fellow, I believe you were the cause of it ' "

The Roads and the River—Complaint

div.head: from Mr. F. Monks.
div.p: from Mr. F. Monks.

Sir,—l wish to call the attention of the prop' r authori- ties to the very bid state of many of Warrington streets, and more especially to the condition of Liverpool-road, Walton New-road, and the streets connecting the two. If it were possib'e to estimate the extra wear and tear upon vehicular traffic it would be found to be a very serious tax in addition to the rates paid for having the work properly done and attmded to. Tne caus3 of all this neglect and consequent expense upon the ratepayers is not far to seek, but individual ratepayers are power- less to remedy it so long as members of the Corporation decline to deal with a difficulty they know to exist. I must also complain of the condition of the river for want of proper dredging. By an agreement with the Manchester Ship Canal Company, the Corporation through its servants have undertaken to deal with this matter, but I must complain publicly of the want of proper attention by the Corporation in seeing that the Ship Canal Company efficiently perform their part of the agreement. We are large ratepayers, and have a right to expect that the Corporation will see that the interests of manufactures are not neglected by its servants. We look to the Mayor and the various committees who have charge of departmental work to see that the officials whom they appoint do their duty to the ratepayers, and if they tail in the performance of their duties, it is Lr them to deal with them without fear or favour. Yours truly,
F. MONKS.
Some anomalies of National Religion

Sir,—There are some strange and startling anomalies connected with the national profession of religion which seem to excite little or no interest in the popular mind, and yet they are of the gravest importance, and deserve the most serious consideration of all who desire to pro- mote peace and goodwill among men. Upon one of these anomalies I will now, with your kind permission, offer a few simple observations hoping, through your favour, to deal with some others on a future occasivn.

In all countries which pose as Christian it is gener- ally, if not universally, acknowledged that there is a God who exercises supreme control over all thinga both in Heaven and on earth. And millions of money are every year expended upon teachers who inculcate, or are sup- posed to inculcate, the doctrine that this God is an eternal Being possessed of infinite knowledge and power and a sure, unfailing refuge and defence for all who put their trust in Him. It will be admitted at once that this is a grand and comforting doctrine, and most gladly do I believe that it is accepted and acted upon by many lowly people of all ranks in life who find to their joy that C.oti is really a present help in time of trouble. And if this could be truly said of the rulers and statesmen who are supposed to represent the people of the Christian nations how different would be the conditions of the woald from what it is to-day; for God delights to honour those who henour him. Nor has he left men without clear and convincing precedents to encourage them to put their trust in him nationally as well as in- dividually. How appalling was the alilemma in which the Israelites found themselves a few days after their departure from Egypt! On the right and left aides ef their encampment towered impassable mountains;in front of them was the Red Sea, and behind the pursuing army of Pharaoh bent on their capture or destruction. No situation could have been more hopeless from a human point of view. And yet their noble leader, strong in the power of faith, counselled no method for defence or escape, but calmly told the alarmed people to "eland still and see the salvation of the Lord." And that salvation was quick and complete. Not a single Israelite was harmed, but the whole of their enemies were miraculously overwhelmed in the depths of the sea ! And an equally striking instance of Divine deliverance securred in the reign of the good King Hezekiate That monaech had been threatened and his God blasphemed by the emissaries of Sennaeherib, King of Assyria. But flezekiati made no response by a call to arms and a gathering of warriosr to defend his capital. No, his trust was in the God of Israel, and his prayer for protectian was answered by the Angel of the Lord going forth and slaying the whole of the Assyrian hoet. And it was this strong, unflinch- ing confidence in the Almighty that inspired the saintly Origen of Alexandria when he penned his famous answer to Celsus. In that remarkable treatise are these words : "We say that if two of us shall agree on earth as touching anything that they shall ask, it shall be done for them of the Father of the Just, , who is in heaven. What then are we to expect, if not only a very few should agree, as at present, but the r whole empire of Rome ? They would pray to the Word, who of old said to the Hebrews, when pursued by the Egyptians, The Lord shall fight for you, and ye shall hold your peace :' and if all should unite in prayer with one accord, they should put to flight enemies far more numerous than were discomfitted by the prayer of Moses, and:of those who prayed with him." How has the simple faith of the Gospel been perverted since Origen died in A.D. 254 ! Whatever effect the inspired records of Divine help may have upon indivi- dual minds, they seem to make little or no impression upon the rulers and bulk of the people in Christian countries. And this national disregard of God is never more apparent than in the time of war. It is true we are accustomed to the impious speccacle of the ministers of religion blessing the troops and putting prayer-cards into their hands ; but whoevet hears of the Christian kings and queens following the example of Moses and Hez•kiah by committing their cause to God ! And so little is that God thought of in Christian Parliaments, that were a senator to rise up in His place and move a rerlntion that Oenendecce upon the Almighty, and not position of Christians, he upOn armawntg:Wigtht." tn 22 ! would, in all probability, be M ndet derision. The truth is that, triSateVnt theories the ' rulers and masses of the people of Christendorn May hold regarding God, faith in Him as a aura refuge and defence is not one of their working principles. Large armies and powerfui fleets are the gods to which they resort in emergencies, and the more efficient they are for destruction the greater is the National self confidence and boasting. And a very remarkable thing about these armies and fleets is that they are neither maintained nor used for defence against the heathen who are supposed to be the great enemies of Christianity. Savages never attempt to grab the land and destroy the people of Christian countries, for they have long since learned, by terrible experience in their own kingdoms, that they are no matcn for the Christian warriors in the arts of destroy- ing life and property. No, the Christian nations are armed to the teeth against one another. Men who pro- fess to believe in the same God and Saviour, and to entertain the same hope of a future life cannot, it seems, dwell side by side in the unity befitting their creed. Ambition, jealousy, avarice and other anti- christian developments often lead to the most horrible wars amongst themselveseas witness Waterloo t he Crimea and the more recent Franco-German conflict ! And to- day the whole heathen world stands aghast at the awful spectacle of British and Dutch Churchmen engaged in a deadly strife in South Africa tor the mastery of territories to which neither party has any really just claim. There are,of course,the usual sickening incidents attending this war, but added to these, each of the combatants blaephemougly declares that God is on their side ! What a strong delusion, and worthy of him who was a liar as well as a murderer from the beginning. When God fights for a people there are no killed and wounded in their ranks as we have seen in the two cases quoted from the Boak that was written for our learning. In the great war led by Joshua there was, indeed, a toga of thirty-six men who fell before their enemies- But it seems that God caused these casualties to happen in order to mark Eis abhorrence of the sin of Achan in coveting and appropriating some of the accursed goods of the Canaanites. But in the present, as well as in all former Christian wars, the casualties on both sides are simply enormous, and prove beyond doubt that God has no part whatever in the fiehting. Brute ferce,aided by superior weapons, is the artiter of all modern wars both Christian and savage. And now for a closing sentence or two. If, what I have written be true, and I believe it is, what is the conclusion fairly deducible from it ? Is it not this, that the present condition of the Christian nations, armed as they are to the teeth, and full of political agitation and unrest, is a standing menace to the whole world, and a flat denial of the doctrine of trust in God. If these nations cannot or will not believe in the Almighty as a sure refuge and defence, they might at least have the honesty to say so, and discontinue the unseerningly practice of paying large salaries to titled ecclesiastics whose profession is to preach the contrary.— Yours truly, lONA.

On Sunday Mr. A Cope of Liverpool, preiched from the 16th of Matthew and 13th verse speiking about a Christian's life. He said it be professes to be saved and does not live a life which corresponds it is of not much u4e. If the Chritian's desire is to live a life like Christ God will work in our hearts in mighty power. When Nic,odemus came to Christ as the representative of the Pharisees, he flattered him with his words but Christ turned to him and said. "Ye must be born again." Christ says be loves us, but he hates our sin. We have only to take a look at Calvary's Cross and there we see a beautiful picture of God's love towards us.

He arrived at Cape Town a few days later, and was taken on board the Dominion liner Canada at Cape Town. The Canada made a magnificent voyage, reaching Southampton ig sixteen and a half days, beating the mail. Lieutenant Pilking- ton expressed his appreciatioa of the kindness of the residents of the locality who assembled at the hall and gave him so hearty a welcome. It was very pleasant to be back in England and in sight of the greea fields once more. With reference to the possibility of the memtrrs of the various Yeo- manry corps settling in South Africa, Lieu- tenant Pilkingten thinks that this will be impracticable in the majority of cases. In a bi,7 country like the Transvaal and Orange River Colony a good deal of capital will be required by intending settlers. As to the probable date of the termination of the war, Mr Puking. ton could give no idea, but he believes the Yeomanry will be on their way home before the end of the year.
Letter from a Warrington Reservist.

The following are extracts from a letter written by Private J El Brookhouse, Bth (Ross's) Mounted Infantry, 2nd North Staff Co., who is now with the Field Forces in South Africa. It is addressed to a "dear friend"from "Springs, Transvaal." The writer formerly lived at Howley, Warrington, and is;a shoemaker :—"Just a few lines to you to let you know that I am still alive and safe and shot proof. We are having a lively time up nere. I can assure you. We have been a fatigue p trty for Lord Roberts's column. It is all very fine to go day after day with your life in your hands, but things will not last much longer. We had one of our men shot dead last week while on patrol duty and we buried him the same day after we returned to camp. I hope I shall not be long before lam back again in Howley. We are here in charge of several mines which the Boers want to retake very badly, and they often give us a look in. But thank God, we are always able to keep what we have taken, and hold our own against the Boers. The other day a Baer prisoner told one of the guard they did not fear any troops as they do the Mounted Infantry. You may have seen U 9 mentioned as Colonel Roes's Mounted Infantry. We took Elands- fontien Rail way Junction. Our orders were to take it at any cost. I can assure you I shall have earned my medal by the time the war is over." It is worthy of mention that Private Brookhouie is a reservist who fought through the last Zulu war, and was one of the detachment that accompanied the late Lord Rosmead, then Sir Hercules Robinson, wnen as High Commissioner he visited the Orange Free State and the Transvaal. He is now going over much the. same ground again, but under different circumstances.

Widnes Policeman at the Front. Private William Shaw, formerly a constable in the Wid.les police force, writing home from South Africa, under date July 28th, to P.C. Worsfield says I am at Kroonstad. just below the Vaal River, where there has been a lot of fighting with the De Wet mob. His brother Pate De Wet, surrendered to our outpost last night with a few of .his burghers. I wish I could get hold of the other beggar. I should like too have one more scrape with them. Perhaps I shall get the chance yet. We shall be lucky dogs if we finish here by Christmas. Roberts is making a stiff fight of it the other side of Pretoria. Birriie's regiment ca:ne in for it rough—nearly all cut up. By the way Biraie, is at the Remount 1):To.:,." Tne writer concludes with beet wishes to all friends. It may be explained that the )3irnie referred to served in the Widces police force Some years.

div.head: WAR.
div.p: THE WAR.
LATEST TELEGRAMS.
Baden-Powell's Engagement De Wet Returning to Orange
River. Guns Buried. Followers Reduced to 300. Steyn Joining Kruger.
The following telegram from Lard Roberts to the Secretary for War was issued yesterday :
PRETORIA, WEDNESDAY 4.35 P .IFT . -
Buller reports that his division marched yesterday to Van Wycks Vlei, 15 miles due south of Belfast. He states there were about 20 casualties, but gives no names.

When Methuen -advanced from the Vaal in pur- suit of De Wet he left Lieutenant-Colonel Yong husband and three sick and wounded men in a farm near Lindeque, under the charge of Captain Powell, R.A.M.C. They are.now sufficiently well to travel, and will be brought to Vereeniging to-morrow. Paget reports froln Unmans Kraal that Biden- Po well was agaged with Commandant Grobelar's rearguard all yesterday. Grobelar was driven back on the east of Piennaar's River, and Baden- Powell occupied the railway station of that name last evening. During the fight Baden- Powell's and the enemy's advance guards galloped into each other. The Rhodesian Reziment suffered severely. Lieutenant-Colonel Spreckley and four men being killed, nnd Lieutenant Irvine and six men wounded ; Captain Kinsman, Royal Dublin Fusiliers, also severely wounded. The Boers lost a good many killed and wounded. Their laager was at Cyferkail, on the Plat River, this morning, and is being closely pursued by Plumer and Hickman.

It seetns pretty certain that De Wet, finding it hopeless to make his way eastward with his guns and wagg3ns has re-crossed the Magalies Berg with a few mounted men, with the intention of returning to the Orange River Colony. Be will arrive there in a very different condition from that in which he started from Bethlehem. Then he had six or eight guns and some 2,000 men with him, and left Prin- Moo with five or six thousand in Bethlehem hills. Between four and five thousand of these are on their way to Ceylon. The guns have mostly been buried and D 3 Wet's personal following cannot amount to much more than 300.
Steyn, with a small bodyguard, is stated to have crossed the Pienaaar's River on his way to join Kruger at Machadodorp.
A LOCAL OFFICER WOUNDED.
Gallant Feat by Captain Reynolds.

Captain Guy P. Reynolds, the third son of the late Captain Reynolds, of Raddon Court, Latchford, and whose mother now resides at Wbatcroft Hall, near Northwich, has recently distinguished him- self in a cavalry patrol in an engagement in South Africa. The official notification of the engagement is as follows : From General Clery (for General Buller) to the Secretary of State for War, , GREYLING-TAD SATURDAY. _ _ .

Captain Reynolds and 22 non-cotnmissioned officers and men of the sth Dragoon Guards took compieely by surprise about 80 of the enemy's force near to Dorukop 14th August. It is believed that enemy's loss is considerable. Captain Rey- nolds.slightly wounded. 1663 Private H Brerchley reported missing. The special correspondent of the " Daily News." writing from Durban, on Saturday, sends the fol- lowing graphic account of the incident :—A smart bit of work has been performed by Captain Rey- nolds, Captain Travers, and twenty men of the sth Dragoon Guards at Botze's Drift, on the Buffalo River. On the 15th inst , learning that a party of the enemy were visiting a farm occupied by Boers who had sworn the oath of neutrality, they went forth to make a reconnaissance. Approaching the farm they advanced on foot, seventeen carbines all told. They found a hundred Boers in laager with no sentries posted, and had got to within 70 yards of the enemy when two Boers rode out challenging them. Captain Reynolds promptly despatched both with a right and a left from his Mauser pistol. Pandemonium ensued, in which the Dragoons did great execution, retiring with one man missing. Captain Reynolds was slightly wounded in the hand, This lesson has had a good effect on the Boers.

It may be added that Captain Reynolds has been through the entire campaign, and took part in the earliest engagement at Elands Laagte. was in Ladysmith as lieutenant during the siege,and after- wards joined General Bailer's force,being promoted to the position of Captain. Readers of the " Ex- aminer " will remember his account of the siege as reconled in the published letters sent home. When in England he was one of the best known followers of the Cheshire Hunt, and his success has been re- ceived with satisfaction by his numerous friends.

div.head: Return of Lieutenant Pilkington, of St. Helens. • The Work of the Lancashire Hussars.
div.p: Return of Lieutenant Pilkington, of St. Helens. • The Work of the Lancashire Hussars.

Lieutenant E. S. Pilkington, eldest son of Colonel R. Pilkington. M.P., who has been on active service in South Africa with the 32n1 Company Imperial Yelmanry (Lancashire Hu,sars), arrived at S. Helens on Tuesday about 7.30 p. n. He was met at the station by several members ot the family, and was cheered by a crowd of 600 or 700 townspeople,who had assembled to give him a welcome. Lieutenant Pilkington has been invalidel home after suffering from fever. Lieutenant and Mrs. Pilking- ton at once drove from the station to their re&dence, Windle Hall, where the tenants and employees had erec• ted a pretty fl-,ral arch,which was illuminated by fairy lamps and lanterns. In conversation with a press repre- sentative Lieutenant Pilkington stated that he left the Lancashire Hussars at Prieska, where they went along with Lord Kitchener arid the 7th Dragoon Guards shortly before the capture of Bloemfontein. The Yeo- manry had been kept busy patrolling the rebel country as far as Uppington, and were in action at Kheis, under Sir Charles Warren They had four men klled in action and several wounded. They also lost six or seven men by enteric fever. Although the men never grumbled they had a prstty rough time, and for three months they had ro tents, and slept in the open, which was very trying. Daring each night they had fiv,i or six degrees of frost, and during the day they were ex posed to a warm, bright sun. Lieutenant Pilkington has been ill since the end of June. He had a severe attack of enteric, which entirely prostrated him

div.head: MILITARY NOTES.
div.p: MILITARY NOTES.

Captain Baynes, the senior company commander of the Ist Volunteer Battalion South Lancanire Regiment at Warrington, will shortly complete 15 years service qualifying for the honorary rank of major in the Volunteer force. fie joined the corps at the end of 1885 and was promoted captain in December 1886,

Brevet Lieutenant Colonel Shskleton, South Lancashire Regimerf;, who has been for some time past employed oa the lines of communication in South Africa has now been formally appointed assistant adjutant general on the staff of Sir F Forrestier Walker in South Africa. He was serving with the Egyptian Army before the occurrence of hostilities: in South Africa and went to the Cape last October when he was appointed a station Com- mandant in Cape Colony. It is anticipated that if all goes well in South Africa the majority of militia battalions will have arrived home by the end of December including the 3rd Battalion South Lancashire Regiment. It is well-known that the whole of the militia is to be retained for service during the autumn and winter and no corps will be disembodied until at the earliest about next March. The 3rd Battalion South Lancashire Regiment was one of the first corps to be embodied, for it assembled at Warrington on 13th December and after b3intrr, located at Preston went to South Africa early in the spring. There will be a difficulty experienced in pro viding quarters for the militia units coming home from South Africa. Many of the battalions now at home will during the autumn and winter be accommoda- ted in the huts which are now being erected at various centres. lam informed on good authority that when the; 3rd Battalion South Lancashire Regiment comes home from South Africa, the Corps will probably be located at Warrington, and that the men will be accommodated for the time in billets.

Captain Skirrow, 3rd battalion South Lancashire Regiment, will it is understood, sbortly be granted the honorary rank of Major in the Militia force. He has over the qualifying period of 15 years service. He joined the Army in. 1883 ; became Captain in the South Lancashire Regiment in 1890 and four years later took his retired pay for the purpose of joining the Militia being appointed Captain in the 3rd battalion with headquarters at Warrington. Lieutenant Stewart, Northamptonshire Regiment, serving on probation in the Army pay department and doing duty in the station pay office at War- rinaton will shortly complete his term of service on probation and will bte appointed paymaster with the provisional rank of captain.

div.head: FARM FATALITY AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: THE FARM FATALITY AT EARLESTOWN.

Mr. S. Brighouse. county coroner, held an inquest in the Town Hall, Earlestown, on Saturday, on the body of George Mort who was killed by a lorry falling on top of him whilst assisting his fathrr to cart hay from the field to the farm on Thur,d ay the 16'h inst. John Mort father of the deceased, said he owned the farm which 't by the name of Heald Farm, Newton-le-Willows, and his son was . six yeara of age last birthday. He and three of his sons including deceasfd were taking a lurry to the hayfield for a load of hay, the eldest of the three lads; leading the horse. He turned away from the lorry to get some oats and left his son to lead the horse up a rather steep hill. The boy, however, st loped the horse half way up the hill and the lorry immediately began to descend the incline dragging the horse with it, and eventually falling down a ditch abou 40ft. deep. The boy who was leading the horse left go when he saw the danger and two of the other boys jumped clear but decea;ed fed underneath the lurry and when picked up was found to have fractured his skull in two places. He died on being carried to the farm.
The jury returned a verdict of" Accidental death."
P.S.A. Society.:—A United Service.

Mr. T. S. Steel some few Sundays ago, when pre- siding at the weekly meeting of the P.S.A., held at the Y.NI.C.A., invited the members to join the St. Peter's Men's service, in a united service some Sun- day afternoon. ' The suggestion was well received, and the CYMMittee of Management made the neces- sary arrangements. Sunday was the day chosen, and the members of the P.S.A. Society met at Friars' Green, and headed by the Borough Band, marched in procession to the church, by way of Bridge-street, Horsemarket-street, Winwick-street, and Pinne,r's Brow to Birch all-street. At the church there was a large congregation. The service,which was of a hearty character, was conducted by the Rev W Bracecamp, and the lesson was read by Mr William Hickman, the president of the P.S.A. Society. The Rev W Bracecamp, in welcoming the members, said that their motto was clasped hands. They at St. Peter's had held out the hand of brother- hood and they had grasped it in return. He gave them a hearty welcome, and trusted that both their societies would benefit by the visit. His address, which was listened to with marked attention, was based upon the words, "Love the brotherhood." The singing, led by the choir, was excellent,and Mr E Llewellyn Pearce sang two solos, in capital style. Mr Fred Webster was at the organ. The service was in all respects a great success,and the members of the P S.A. expressed a hope that when the men of St. Peter',, Church paid them the return visit the gathering would be equally successful.
