div.head: HAYDOCK COLLIERY DISASTER.
div.p: THE HAYDOCK COLLIERY DISASTER.
The Use of Naked Lights.
Inquest and Verdict.

0 a Monday morning, at the Waggon and Horses Hotel, Haydock, Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, held the inquest on the bodies of the eight men who had suc- cumbed to the terrible injuries they received in the ex- plosion in the 0:d Huston Colliery, Haydock, owned by Messrs. Richard Eva us and Co.. on the 29:h June last The brief facts of the occurrence are that ten men were engaged in sinking operations at the bottom of the shaft, when a sudden rush of escaping gas was ignited by the naked candles which were being used. and a ter- rific explosion followed. All the workers were shockingly burned, and they were removed to the Haydock Cottage Hospital. At varying periods, subse- quently, no fewer than eight of the poor fellows expired from the effects of their injaries the names and addresses of the victims being James (Allard, 45 years of age, Legh-street, Earlestown ; Patrick Babe, 40 years of age, of 41, Barb.r.street St. Helens ; James King, 20 years of age, of 312, Church-road, Haydock ; Patrick Flaherty, 35 years of age, of 19, Res.rvoir-st., Ashton-in- Makerfield ; James Hynes, 33 years of age, of 83, Athol street, Earlestown ; Patrick King, 26 years of age, brother of the deceased James King, of Church-road, Haydock ; John Fitzpatrick, 28 years of age. of 1 Heath. street, Asnton-in Makerfield ; and Mark Luke, 52 years of age. of 139, Legh-street, Earlestown. In each case the coroner held formal inquiries, and heard evidence of identification in order to be enabled ta give burial certi- ficates, the general inquiry into the circumstances of the explosion being adjeurned until last Monday. At the opening of the inquest, Mr 111 Hall, Governm■nt inspector of mines, and Mr. T. Glover, J,P., St. Helens, miners' agent, were present. Messrs. Richard Evans and Co. were represented by Mr T R Ellis, solicitor, of the firm of Messrs Peace and Ellis (Wigan), and there were present Mr William K.llett consblting engineer, of the firm of Messrs. Kellett,Ellis, and Kellett (Wigan) ; Mr John Robinson. general manager for the firm ; and Mr James Cook., certificated manager of Old B ,ston Colliery. Mr H L Riley, solicitor, St. Hdens, attended on behalf of the next-if-kin of the deceased intn Babe, the two Kings, Fitzpatrick, and Hynes. Police-inspector King was pre3ent on belhalf of the police authorities.
Mr. John Robinson, the general mana.zer, produce-I plans of the scone of the explo3ion,both befoTe and after the occurenc3, which he explained to the °lroner and jury. _

Tnomas Walsh. a colliery sinker, of Fairclough-street, Earlestown, said he was working ?or Mr. Joseph Morris, contractor. Ashton-in-Makerfield, who had charge of the sinking operations, in the shaft of the Old Boston Colliery at the time of the explosion. There were ten men in the" shift," and they started work at ten o'clock on the previous night. Mark Luke, one of the men who had died, was the chargeman of the shift. The explo- sion happened about five o'clock in the morning. They were filling hoppets with dirt and sending them to the top of the shaft. About *. wo o'clock in the morning ten " shots " for blasting the stuff were fired. While the shots were being fired the men had their supper and then resumed work. They had both electric light and caked candles—probably half a dozen of the latter, which were fixed to the sides of the shaft. He could not say whether anyone examined the bottom of the shaft after the shots had been fired to see whether it was safe or not for toe men Eo resurll4 work.—ln reply to Mr Hall,witness said he ' had been a pit sinker for over 20 years. They had used ' the electrie light ever since they started sinking in the shaft. He could net say when naked candles were first used. To the best of his judgment the naked liehts were brought in the chair, to give them a better light at the sides of the shaft when they were drilling for the abet-holes. Witness could' not say whether any safety lamp was taken to the bottom between the firing, of the shots and the explosion. He had not beard of any gas having been noticed in the shaft during the whole of the sinking operations.—Mr. Hall : I want you to tell me what were your sensations when this happened.—Wit- ness : The first thing I noticed was the heaving of the ground, It did not make a gvat report. Just then the blaze broke out, and I was thrown flat on my face at the side of the shaft. In the blaze I could not tell what occurred, but I saw the m,n on the opposite side of the sh'aft, and I tried to get to them. I got hold of the chain of the hoppet, and found it was red-hot, with the result that my fingers were burnt, All of the men and myself were afterwards taken up the shaft in the hoppet.—ln reply to further questions by Mr. Hall, witness said the blaze appeared a second or two after the heaving of the ground. The candles were about 4ft. from the bottom of the shaft.—By Mr. Riley He did not know by whose suggestion it was that the naked candles were taken down the shaft. He could not tell whether they were used on the instruction of the company or of the contractor. The fuses of the "shots" were lit by the candles. He did not see any safety lamp taken down to find if there was any gas about.—ln reply to Mr. E lis, witness said that before the explosion he heard a alight" fizzing," as if there , was an escape. He did not cal' anybody's attention to ' it, because he had heard similar noises on former occasions,and bad taken no notice of them. He admitted having seen the warning notices to sinkers, but had never read them. The Coroner: Would it not have been better if you had drawn attention to the noise that von heard ?—Witness : I might have been insulted it I had mentioned it. —The Coroner: Bit you had better be insulted than killed.—Witness said he would certainly have called attention to the noise if he had thought there was any danger. He had heard similar noises before and nothing had happened, and be thought nothing about it at the time, _

Luke. Dill n, the other survivor, of Queen-street, Got- borne, said he was steadvirsg the hornet when the flame of the explosion shot out. He turned to the pit sile and pulled his cap over his face. He was tumbled over by some of the men knocking against him, and he lay still on the ground until the flame had disappeared. He then saw the other men trying to get into the hoppet, and he assisted one or two to do to. They were all drawn to the top. Witness said that when they were engaged in sinking operations the men did not know how far they were from the coal. Before the accident he heard gas was going off, but he dil net think it was of much im- portance. He had heard similar escapes or jets of gas going off in most of the pits in which he had worked. He had never seen any of the officials or any one making an examination at the bottom of the shaft for gas, He had seen safety lamps down the shaft.—ln reply to Mr. Riley, he said he was certain all the ten shots prepared before the accident had fired. He counted the holes himself.—By Mr. Glover : It was usual for Mark Luke, the chargman, one of the men killed, to evamine the spot after shots had been fired He could not say whether he did so on that particular occasion. The electric light was too far away from them to give sufficient light for the work the men had to do. He understocid that the lamp could not be lowered at the time in coestion.—ln answer to Mr. Ellis, he said he pointed out the escape of gas to Mark Luke. No extra precautions =ere taken because none of the men thought they were necessary. Mr. James Cooke, the certificated manager of the c,lliery, said the shaft at the time of the accident was 2 and had a diameter cf 18 feet. Naked4ssardli: n pt hits had never ever been prohibited, and were not intr -duced because the electric light could not be mov rd. After the shots had been fired it was the duty of the charge man to descend with another man to examine the place Luke was an experienced man and knew the rules. If, as previous witnesses had testified, no one examined the place before the men resumed work after the shots had been fired, them was something amiss Had he been there and heard the hissing he would have had every light put nut. After the accident he paw Luke and the other men, and asked if h. had heard anything. Luke replied in the negative, and the rest did not offer a contradictory statement. If there was any fault it lay with the chargeman in not carrying nut the rules. The men used the candles with his consent, Three pits had been sunk at the colliery with candles Mr. Hall : You take the resnrinsibility for having can- dles used—no one interferes with you ?-I.Virness : No one interferes with me.—Continuing his evidence, he sail he had never known an upheaval of that kind in a sinking pit before. Charles .Inhaosen. of 106, Ashcrnfr..:treet, St Heilens,a banksinare ; Hugh Nearer, of 64. Gerard-s-recit, Ashton: in-Maxerfield, assistant banksman ; and John Jones, of Powfall, the charge man on the previous " shift," also (rare evidence in accordance with the testimony of pre- vious witnesaes.

Mr. H. Hall, the GovernManr inspector, said he had visited r he scene of the explosi in. He found there had been a considerable upheaval, hut it was difficult to say when it took place. The natural time would be when the shots fired, hit after considering the whole of the circumstances he had come to the conclusion that the gas would have fired immediately the men descended in the bonnet. The rule was that the place ought to have been examined before the men were allowed to go down. The manager had it entirely withia his discretion as to wh -ther candles or safety lamps should be us-d in sink- ing. It dependad anon what he thought to hr 3 the char- acter of the seam. The character of that particular seam was admittedly fiery, for at one or two of Messrs Evans's collieries it had been found to give off a deal of gas, so that the manager would be hound. as he approached the seam, to use safely lamps. The manager had told them that he intended to do so, hut the time flan n-t arrived when he thought it nice sary. What had led up to the explosion was the fact that Mark (Juke had not made an examination immediately after the shots had fired, and the fact that the naked liahts were pu" into the pit. It did not follow that because he did not make the examination the accident occurred, be- cause it ha•menod three hours later ; but the chances were that if an examination had been made 'within three hours of the shot firing, in all probability there %you'd have been found some gas already orzing out. He thought it showed a want of judgment on tha part of the chief officials that they did not, when they knew they were sinking the shaft Bo considerably, make all their men use electric lights or aafetylamps. He thought it was indiscreet to use candles at that particular

depth, knowing that the seam of coal was so near. Colliery managers seemed to cling to the old naked lights ' in sinking pits, and nearly all the accidents in that part of the district had arisen from that cause. He thought as ele‘:tricity was so cheap, that the time had arrival when, in sinking pits and reaching any great depth, operations should be carried out by electric lights. This concluded the evidence, and the Coroner, in leaving the facts to the jury. said it was for them to decide upon the evidence.and to say whether or not the occurrence was an accident, and to make any recom- mendation that they considered necessary. The jury after a brief consultation, returned a verdict of " Accidental death "in each case, brought about by a sudden outbreak of gas. Taey recommended that in future all sinking op!ratims shJuld be camel out by electric light.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. Rugby Football.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. Rugby Football.
[By " Ovalist.l

Football resumes iti sway over the sports-loving Public from Saturday next and for eight months onward. Cricket will not entirely have deserted the greensward, but what there is left of the summer pastime will assuredly have to take a back seat in general interest. For weeks both Rugby and Association organizations have bean working their hardest to perfect arrangements and mak a good start, which, as I have said b3fore, is half the battle. Some teams invariably make a good beginning to the season's work, others commence by failure which takes a lot of recovering from

Warrington it one of the clubs which usually enters on the aeason in a state of sufficient unpreparednesa to blast their chances for good and all. Why this should be so one cannot tell. There have been occasions when the Committee's dilatoriness has been the cause, but of Late the members of the Committee have spared neither pains nor trouble to get off the mark well. Success has not yet attended eheir efforts, but there is always hope. and I,for ene, hope fervently that this season the club will put well behind it the poor records of the past. It is impossible to over-estimate the importance of getting a firm footing for the fray at the first outset. Every competing team is supposed to have the championship in view. With some, that pros- pect is hopeless, but I will never admit that Warrington is a case in point. There are better teams,certainly,but the best teams do not always come out at the top, and an average combination like that of the Warrington club has a very fair chance if the goal is kept in view from the start. How far would Warrington have been from the top, in several instances, if half the season had not been spent in atoning for the blunders at the com- mencement ? Nat more than a place or two, I swear.

And now as to the team's preparedness. It must at once bo admitted that there is room for improvement, alai the improvement may come in time for the opening match. Most of the players have signed on and are already paying attention to physical form, hut one or two are absent and others have not yet turned out. The skipper is OOP of the, latter, but those who know J. T. Bate well, believe that he will not be found absent from his post when the time comes. He loves the game and the club, and I am firmly convinced that he can be relied upon to stick to both. Jones is one of the absentees,and whither he has goae no man kno cos. He may have to be dis- nens,d with, but in his place there ought to be Landaff Smith who is anxious to come back to the fold he deserted. We could well do with him, fer Smith can fill the crntre position admirably if he wishes. Common sense was what he lacked most last year, and perhaps he will have learnt some in his absence. Fish and Isherwood are reperted to be in good trim ; the former having improved his speed on the path during the summer. "Johnny " ought to be a thorn in the side of his foes this season. Burgos seems better than ever in practice, and there is a chance of Harris qualifying again for the vacant wing position. Hallam is ready to act as c.rstodian, and in addition will probably have, as understudy, Farrimond of Tyldesley. Several youngsters from Altrincham and other clubs are also being tried. The working-clause at present presents difficulties, and I councel the officers and committee to redouble their exertions and get all their men working and turn out on Saturday a comple'e fifteen. A team thus composed and starting with determination ought to improve on previous ventures.

Widnes, our first opponents, will be a hard nut to crack away from home, but they ought to be beaten, dependent as they are on players past their prime. Half- back is a weak place at Widnes, and the three-quarters, with the exce,Jtion of Bown, are not the men they were. During the month there are three matches away out of five, but for all that, last season's record should be improved upon, as Widnes, and the two home games, Salford and St. Helens, were all lost. Surely we can turn those rablcs this timq. It will ts a big disap- pointment to everybody if such is not the case.

div.head: Cricket.
div.p: Cricket.
Warrington had a" day-off" on Saturday, as no fix- ture had been arranged for either first or sAcond teams. Consequently there is nothing to record with regard to their doings.

Sankey Wire Mills engaged High I.4gh on the ground of the latter. The home team went to the wickets fire and were all out for 112. The wire mills compiled 114 for the loss of three wickets—a creditable performance. Evans knocked up 40, not out, for the winners.
Fairfield defeated St. PAUIP, after an interestinz va.me, by a majority of 13 runs, the total.' ben cr 39 and 26 re— spectively. There was no scoring worthy of note on either side.
Grappenhall inflicted a severe drubbing on Sanke9 Wesleyan, knocking up 84 to their opponents 24. War- burton bowled in fine style for the winners, and per- formed the " hat-trick."
Mersey Mills gained an easy victory over Appleton, their innings realising 49 whilst the Appletol team com- piled only 25 runs. P. Johnson was the most useful batsman his score being 19 runs.

Arpley defeated Hope Foundry by a majvritv of 65 runs and two wickets. D. Plinston bowled well for the winners, taking eieht wickets fn* five runs. The totals were Hope Foundry 12, Arpley 77 (for eight wickets).

div.head: Athletics.
div.p: Athletics.

The aports in cangection with the Warrington Foot- ball Club which took place on Saturday were a pro- nennced success. The weather was extremely favourable and was a striking contrast to the wretched climatic conditions associated with Bank HoPday Monday. The atteadance on Saturday was scarcely so large as is generally the case on Bank Holiday, but, nevertheless, considering that the sports were a postponed event, the gate was very satisfactory. There were one or two little mistakes during the afternoon which necessitated a delay. For instance, the measuring of the ground seems to have been done in a rather perfunctory manner. In the 100 yards handicap the distance was found to be too short, whereas in the 220 yards race, it had been over- measured. It was not until six heats of the opening sprint had been run that the time-keeper discovered that the competitors v.ere doing the supposed 100 yards in an amazingly short time and it was found that the course was too short by 10 yards. The usual objections fol- lowed and the heats had to be run over again. In the one mile bicycle handicap, the judges were obliged to stop the race owing to the " crawline2 " which distinguished the opening of the final. The boxing competition was not as great a SUC3FSS as bad been anticipated, for of the 13 entrants only three were found to be of the stipulated weight. F Thompson, the winner, was severely punished by Sweeney but pulled through successfully and also suc- needed in beating Fa;rclongh, of St. Flelens, in the fins!. It was not until the finqers of St. James's Church clock pointed to seven o'clock that the 'last event was con- cluded. A word of praise is due to the officials for the manner in which they discharged their duties.

div.head: Angling.
div.p: Angling.

The first fishing match promoted by Mr Joseph Read, landl, rd of the Howley Hotel, Warrington, was trought to a satisfactory conclusion last week ecd at Vale Royal. 20 competitors entered for the six prizes which were offered. The journey was made by 'bus, and thc weather though very dull and threatening early in the morning, improved as the party neared their destination and a very enjoyable time was spent. The ground having been staked out by Messrs P. Clare and J. Hackney, the draw for position was proceeded with. The march was of two houra duration and as several amateurs had entered the competition much amusement was caused by their novel wave of capturing their fish, one of them being so anxious to land one that when he had got a bite he gave such a pull at the line as to throw the fish in the middle of an ad- joining field. S. Walker ("two-penny"),who was greatly fancied for the premier prize (and who was supplied with " special match lines " &c., by a noted maker) was very unfortunate, as he never caught a fish. The following are the prize winners with the respentive weights of fish caught Jotn Crooks. 13ozs. ; 2nd, George Spencer, 103z5. 91rms. ; 3rd, William Leigh, 1101zs. ; 4'h. James Crooks, 8 Z 9. 2drms. ; sth, John Hackney, 7ilzs. The 6th prize was divided between W. Horwich and E. Berry, senr., each having caught 6Dz3. 2 Irmo.
